he is called the noble assembly. Sariputra, all that is unwholesome, all that is knowable, all that is obtainable — all such unwholesome dharmas as these have names and marks as their
root
, and in this noble Dharma the
severing of
the names and marks [is established].
Again, if one does not think of names and marks, and does not obtain names and marks, how then can one say this is noble and this is an assembly? Cutting off the names and marks
one is called the noble assembly
If there were a place of dharma
something that could be broken and cut off, then in the noble Dharma [it would apply]. But there is no name, no mark, no speech; cutting off all speech
there is no union and no separation. If one says there is no Sangha, then this is to break the noble assembly, which also is unobtainable.
Again, if one does not think of names and marks,
and does not
obtain names and marks,
how can one say this
is noble,
this
is an assembly (
would this not be
a name and mark)? One should know that whoever cuts off the names and marks is called the noble assembly.
It is only
where there is a dharma
that
something can be broken and cut off. But in the noble Dharma there is no name, no mark, no speech; cutting off all speech
there is no union and no separation. If one says there is no Sangha, then to break the noble assembly is also not
obtainable

What are called names and marks — because of false thinking, one is attached to various wrong views. Because of these wrong views, one again receives a future body. Being attached to the various views, the five aggregates arise. Sariputra, the five aggregates are all false attachment; this is called the evil path, this is called wrong view. The noble assembly has no such matter; it only knows that because of the false and deluded, the three realms arise. Knowing this matter, it is called the noble assembly.
What are called names and marks —
this is
false thinking
the reason
for it; because of it one is attached to various wrong views. Because of
these

wrong views, one then goes through birth-and-death (again receiving a future body). Being attached to the various views, the five aggregates arise. Sariputra, the five aggregates are all false attachment; this is called the evil path, this is called wrong view. The noble assembly
has
no such matter; it only knows that because of the false and deluded
there are
the three realms. Knowing
such
a
matter
for this reason
it is called the noble assembly.

"The five aggregates" (skt. skandha): that is, the five heaps — form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. These are the five great elements constituting body and mind. Among them the aggregate of form is the physical body, and the other four aggregates (feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness) are mind. "The three realms": the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the realm of formlessness. The realm of desire is the world where beings possessed of the two desires of sexuality and food dwell, including from the six heavens of desire above, through humans and animals in the middle, down to the hungry ghosts and hells. The realm of form is the world where beings without the two desires of sexuality and food but still possessing a body of form dwell, including the eighteen heavens of the four form-absorption stages. The realm of formlessness is the world where beings no longer have a body of form but dwell with mind-consciousness in the profound and subtle meditation-concentrations, including the four heavens of emptiness (the heaven of the infinity of space, the heaven of the infinity of consciousness, the heaven of nothingness, and the heaven where there is neither thought nor non-thought). These three realms are all the sphere of the birth-and-death of ordinary beings; therefore the first aim of the Buddhist practitioner is to get beyond the three realms.

Sariputra, all views whatsoever are unobtainable within the noble assembly, namely the view of self, the view of beings, the view of a life-span, the view of a person; the view of male and the view of female, the view of the heavens and the view of hell, the view of animals and the view of hungry ghosts, the views of the aggregates, entrances, and elements; the view of the conch's sound and the view of the drum's sound, the views of the sounds of earth, water, fire, and wind; the view of the sound of keeping the precepts and the view of the sound of breaking the precepts; the view of the sound of the right path and the view of the sound of the wrong path; the view of the sound of the defiled and the view of the sound of the pure; the views of the sounds of meditation-concentration and the three samadhis and the eightfold noble path; the views of the sounds of the fruit of the stream-enterer, the fruit of the once-returner, the fruit of the non-returner, and the fruit of the arhat; the view of the sound of liberation and the view of the sound of obtaining the fruit; the view of the sound of the Buddha, the view of the sound of the Dharma, and the view of the sound of the Sangha; the view of the sound of extinction and the view of the sound of nirvana. Sariputra, these are called the views of false sounds and the like. The noble assembly does not obtain these views within the ultimate truth; it penetrates that the various sounds are of a single mark, so-called the mark of no mark. With nothing opposing and nothing contending, accomplishing the acceptance of the Dharma without inversion, it is called the noble assembly.

Sariputra, all views whatsoever are unobtainable within the noble assembly, namely the view of self, the view of a person, the view of beings, the view of a life-span; the view of male and the view of female, the view of the heavens and the view of hell, the view of animals and the view of hungry ghosts, the views of the aggregates, entrances, and elements; the view of the conch's sound and the view of the drum's sound, the views of the sounds of earth, water, fire, and wind; the view of the sound of keeping the precepts and the view of the sound of breaking the precepts; the view of the sound of the right path and the view of the sound of the wrong path; the view of the sound of the defiled and the view of the sound of the pure; the views of the sounds of meditation-concentration and the three samadhis and the eightfold noble path; the views of the sounds of the fruit of the stream-enterer, the fruit of the once-returner, the fruit of the non-returner, and the fruit of the arhat; the view of the sound of liberation and the view of the sound of obtaining the fruit; the view of the sound of the Buddha, the view of the sound of the Dharma, and the view of the sound of the Sangha; the view of the sound of extinction and the view of the sound of nirvana. Sariputra, all these are the views of false sounds and the like. The noble assembly does not obtain
these
views within the ultimate truth; it penetrates that the various sounds
are all
of a single mark, so-called the mark of no mark. With nothing opposing and nothing contending, accomplishing the acceptance of the Dharma without inversion
, it is
called the noble assembly.
Aggregates
(yin),
entrances
(ru),
elements (jie): that is, the five aggregates
(five heaps)
, the twelve entrances (the six roots and six objects)
and
the eighteen elements (the six roots, six objects, and six consciousnesses)
. The six roots: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The six objects
form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharma
The six consciousnesses
eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness
The eightfold noble path
: it is composed of eight mutually related parts, forming a method of cultivation that gets free of suffering and affliction
and
transcends birth-and-death

, being a method of cultivation: First, right view: that is, correct knowledge and vision. Second, right thought: correct thinking. Third, right speech: right words. Fourth, right action: right conduct. Fifth, right livelihood: right occupation or way of living. Sixth, right effort: right diligence. Seventh, right mindfulness: right recollection. Eighth, right concentration: right meditative absorption.

Sariputra, this acceptance of the Dharma without inversion is itself no-mark. Because it is no-mark, there is no taking and no abandoning, no going against and no conforming, no arising and no ceasing. Within it, one naturally tends to extinction, with nothing to cultivate and nothing to destroy, nothing to arise and nothing to obtain, not discriminating this from that; therefore the mind ever dwells in relinquishment. Why? In this acceptance there is no near shore and no far shore, no discrimination and no non-discrimination
Penetrating no-mark, accomplishing this acceptance, one is called the noble assembly
Because one breaks union and combination, one is called the noble assembly.
Sariputra,
this
acceptance of the Dharma without inversion is itself no-mark. Because it is no-mark

there is no taking and no abandoning, no going against and no conforming, no arising and no ceasing. Within this, one naturally tends to extinction, with nothing to cultivate and nothing to destroy, nothing to arise and nothing to obtain, not discriminating this from that;
therefore
the mind ever dwells in relinquishment. Why is this? In this acceptance of the Dharma without inversion, there is no near shore and no far shore, no discrimination and no non-discrimination
Penetrating no-mark, accomplishing this acceptance, one is called the noble assembly
Because one
breaks
union and combination
one is called the noble assembly (because
within the ultimate truth,
union and non-union are both unobtainable).

Sariputra, I have taught in other sutras: if a person sees the Dharma, that is seeing me. The Tathagata is neither Dharma nor non-Dharma. Why? The foolish Devadatta and the various sectarians all see the Buddha by the body of form. Sariputra, the Tathagata should not be seen by the body of form, nor should he be seen by sound. Sariputra, if a person sees the Buddha by the body of form, that is to be far from the Buddha. Why? The Buddha is not called one who sees the form and is said to see the Buddha.
Sariputra, I have said in other sutras: if a person sees the Dharma, that is seeing me (seeing the Buddha).
Yet

the Tathagata is neither Dharma nor non-Dharma. Why? The foolish Devadatta and the various sectarians all see the Buddha by the body of form. Sariputra, the Tathagata should not be seen by the body of form,
nor
should he be seen by sound. Sariputra, if a person
comes
to see the Buddha by the body of form, this
is to be
far
from
the Buddha
and to go further away. Why is this? Because the Buddha does not
say that
seeing
the Buddha's
body
of form is called seeing the Buddha.
"Devadatta" (Tiaoda)
, also translated
Ti-p'o-ta-to,

the son of King Dronodana, the elder brother of Ānanda, and the cousin (paternal cousin) of Śākyamuni Buddha. He left home to study transcendent powers, was endowed with the thirty marks, and recited the sixty thousand collections of Dharma. For sake of fame and gain he committed the three rebellious offenses (breaking the harmony of the sangha, drawing blood from the Buddha's body, and killing the Bhikshuni Utpalavarna), and at death fell into hell.

Sariputra, if a person can see that all dharmas are without mark, without name and without touch, without recollection and without thought, without arising and without ceasing, without idle discourse, not thinking of any Dharma, not thinking of nirvana, not taking nirvana as an object of thought, not greedy for nirvana, believing and understanding that all dharmas are of a single mark, so-called the mark of no mark — Sariputra, this is called truly seeing the Buddha. The Buddha declares that all dharmas are without seeking, without idle discourse, without arising, and within this matter one neither thinks nor discriminates; this is called seeing the Buddha. If a person within this Dharma is without recollection, thought-making, and discrimination, without taking and abandoning, without greed and without opposition, without thought and without the activity of thought, not greedy for speech, knowing that Dharmas are but provisional names, all without any substance, cutting off the path of speech, without division or difference, and without idle discourse — this is called a practitioner of non-arising and non-thought, and within the world he is called the noble assembly.

Sariputra, if a person can see that all dharmas are without mark, without name and without touch, without recollection and without thought, without arising and without ceasing, without idle discourse, not thinking of any Dharma, not thinking of nirvana, not taking nirvana as an object of thought, not greedy for nirvana, believing and understanding that all dharmas are of a single mark, so-called the mark of no mark — Sariputra,
this
is called truly
rightly
seeing the Buddha. The Buddha
says
that all dharmas are without seeking, without idle discourse, without arising
and ceasing
, and within this matter one neither thinks nor discriminates; this is called
truly

seeing the Buddha. If a person within this Dharma is without recollection, thought-making, and discrimination, without taking and abandoning, without greed and without opposition, without thought and without the activity of thought, not greedy for speech, knowing that Dharmas are but provisional names, all without any substance, cutting off the path of speech, without division or difference, and without idle discourse — this is called a practitioner of non-arising and non-thought, and within the world he is called the noble assembly.
Sariputra, because of seeing what Dharma is one called seeing the Buddha? It is so-called no-thought

no discrimination, no idle discourse, not receiving any Dharma. If by the gate of emptiness, the gate of extinction, or the gate of detachment, one does not think to see and does not obtain to see, this matter also is unobtainable — that is, the name ["see the Buddha"]; in this place what is called nirvana is also unobtainable. Why? Sariputra, I do not even think of nirvana — how could I say that you should think of nirvana and should obtain nirvana?
Sariputra, because of seeing what Dharma
's reason
is one called seeing the Buddha? It is so-called:
all dharmas
as no-thought
no discrimination, no idle discourse, not receiving any Dharma.
Because all dharmas are empty, all dharmas are extinct, all dharmas are detached from marks
therefore
one does not think to see and does not obtain to see;
this
matter (not thinking to see and not obtaining to see) is also unobtainable
, being a mere provisional name
, and in this place what is called nirvana is also unobtainable. Why? Sariputra, I
do not even
think of nirvana,
how could I
say that you should think of nirvana and should obtain nirvana

Sariputra, if a person [thinks he] has obtained nirvana, that person has not gone forth following the Tathagata but has gone forth following the six sectarian teachers. Sariputra, one should know that this person is a thief of the Dharma who has entered into my Dharma; one should know that this person defiles my Dharma; one should know that this person is a great thief, as in a great city there may be a great thief. Why? Such a deluded person does not even obtain nirvana, much less a self or a person!
Sariputra, if
a
person
supposes himself
to have obtained nirvana,
this
person has not
in fact
gone forth following the Tathagata,
but has

gone forth following the six sectarian teachers. Sariputra, one should know that this person is a thief of the Dharma who has entered into my Dharma; one should know that this person defiles my Dharma; one should know that this person is a great thief, as in a great city there may be a great thief. Why is it
said
so? Such a deluded person does not at all know that nirvana is not even obtainable, much less the self or a person
"The six teachers" (six sectarians): the six relatively powerful non-Buddhist schools in the central Indian region during the Buddha's lifetime.

Sariputra, such a deluded person — I ward him off with my hand; he is not my disciple, he does not enter into the count of the assembly, and I am not his teacher. Sariputra, if one knows that all dharmas are unarisen and unceasing, without thought and without marks, and obtains this acceptance, he does not even obtain nirvana, much less self or person! Sariputra, what the Buddha speaks is thus called seeing the Dharma; one able to see this matter is called seeing the Buddha. Sariputra, what is called a Buddha? All dharmas as thusness, not different and not destroyed, is called the Tathagata. If a person within this Dharma has no doubt and no regret, he is called the noble assembly.

Sariputra, such a deluded person — I ward him off with my hand; he is not my disciple, he does not enter into the count of the assembly, and I am not his teacher. Sariputra, if one knows that all dharmas are unarisen and unceasing, without thought and without marks, and obtains
this
acceptance, he realizes that nirvana is not even obtainable, much less self or person! Sariputra, what the Buddha speaks is thus called seeing the Dharma; one able to see
this
matter, is called seeing the Buddha. Sariputra, what is called a Buddha? All dharmas as thusness, not different and not destroyed, is called the Tathagata. If a person within
this
Dharma has no doubt and no regret, he is called the noble assembly.
[All dharmas are thus] — all dharmas
are neither two nor different;
“thus” is the sense of sameness.

“Shariputra, in a past life, there was a deluded man who did not recognize monkeys. He entered a great forest and saw a troop of monkeys gathered together in one place. This man had heard that there was the Trayastrimsha heaven, and so he took them to be the gods of Trayastrimsha. Straightway he left the forest and returned to his own village, and

in the midst of a great many people he spoke thus: ‘Have you ever seen the Trayastrimsha heaven?’ All the people answered, ‘We have never seen it.’ Thereupon he said, ‘I have already seen it. Do you wish to see it?’ They all said they wished to see it. Thereupon he led the great assembly to that forest and showed them the troop of monkeys, saying,

‘Behold these gods of Trayastrimsha.’ All the people said, ‘These are not the gods of Trayastrimsha; these are monkeys that delight to dwell in the forest. Because you are deluded and inverted you do not recognize monkeys, and you also do not recognize the gods of Trayastrimsha.’ Shariputra, this man vainly led the great assembly to that forest.”

noble assembly, and to hear the Dharma?’ Among them, laypeople who believe in the Dharma will all say they wish to see and to hear the Dharma.”
Just like the deluded man who did
not recognize the heavenly princes
of Trayastrimsha, Shariputra, in
the future there will be bhikshus
who do not recognize the Dharma, and
who go among laypeople and say:
‘Do you wish to see the Buddha and
the noble assembly, and to hear the
Dharma?’ Those laypeople who
believe in the Dharma all say: ‘We wish
to see the Buddha and the noble
assembly, and to hear the Dharma.’

“Shariputra, among them are laypeople who delight in speech who enter the stupas and monasteries, where there are bhikshus fond of discourse, who can pass through all the scriptures, who rely upon words and delight in adornment. These shramanas speak in accordance with them, and declare this to be the true path. They but fill the number of the assembly like cowherds; they merely delight in reading the scriptures, they do not enter the true reality, they only please the minds of men, they value fame and profit, they are skilled in worldly affairs, they preach the Dharma impurely, they are only able to speak cleverly, they practice the worldly path, they have no majesty or virtue, they destroy the cause of nirvana, they abandon the noble silence, they do not delight in meditative concentration, and day and night they are constantly fond of discussion and dispute, sleeping on thick bedding. Not even a single thought is in accord with meditative concentration—how much less could they attain the fruit of the shramana! This man’s sleep is always in accord with the worldly mind; in the first and last watches of the night he does not cultivate acquiescence, and he delights in inferior dharmas.”
Shariputra, among them are laypeople who delight in speech who enter the
stupas and monasteries, where there are many bhikshus fond of discourse,
who can pass through all the scriptures, who rely upon words, and who
delight in embellishing their speech. Thereupon these shramanas, in
accordance with those who delight in speech, preach to them, saying this
is the true path. In fact, these shramanas are mere impostors filling the
count, like cowherds (like cowherds who have no cattle of their own,
a simile for those who preach the path without recognizing the path and
without practicing the path); they merely delight in reading the scriptures,
and do not actually practice; they only please men and value fame
and profit, adept at managing worldly relationships, they preach impurely,
relying only on clever words, treading the worldly path (secularizing
and vulgarizing the Dharma), without majesty or virtue; they destroy
the cause of nirvana, and abandon the noble Dharma and tranquility; they
do not delight in meditative concentration, and day and night are constantly
fond of discussion and dispute, greedy for comfort and ease. Not
even a single thought accords with meditative concentration—how much less
could they attain the fruit of the shramana! This man is greedy for
sleep, always in accord with the worldly mind, and in the first and last
watches does not cultivate acquiescence, delighting in inferior dharmas.

[First watch and last watch] In ancient Indian timekeeping, a day and night is divided into six periods: three periods of day and three periods of night. The three periods of day are the morning, midday, and sunset; the three periods of night are the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch. So one of their periods is equivalent to four modern hours, and six periods are the modern twenty-four hours. The middle watch corresponds roughly to ten at night until two in the morning. The first watch corresponds roughly to six in the evening until ten at night, and the last watch corresponds roughly to two in the morning until six.

“This man also obtains many offerings of clothing, food, and drink. Why is that? Because this man is constantly held by evil demons, delights in shallow and near-at-hand speech, cannot diligently study the ultimate meaning, cannot recite and hold the ultimate profound scriptures; when he hears them he is startled and fearful, and forsaking the rich essence he takes the dregs. There are worldly people who, seeing that he gains profit and support, give rise to a mind of greed and clinging, and think thus: ‘We too should study these doctrines.’”
This man also obtains many offerings of clothing,
food, and drink. Why is that? Because this man is
constantly held by evil demons, and delights in shallow
and near-at-hand words, cannot diligently study the
ultimate meaning, cannot recite and hold the ultimate
profound scriptures; hearing them he is startled and
fearful, and forsaking the essence he takes the
dregs. There are many worldly people who, seeing that
they gain fame and profit, give rise to a mind of greed
and clinging, and think thus: ‘We too should study
these doctrines, and so gain both fame and profit.’
“Shariputra, this man forsakes the unsurpassed treasure of the Dharma, and falls into wrong views; he is a candala among shramanas. There are
laypeople who go to his place, and such an evil man preaches the Dharma to them. For the sake of profit and support he praises the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Sangha; he but seeks to sustain his life as a slave to wealth, greedy for clothing and food, and he praises what he himself delights
in: ‘If one practices giving, one is reborn in heaven.’ But within the Buddha’s Dharma, giving is an inferior dharma, yet he praises it as the
highest, and says: ‘Through the cause of great giving one is born in heaven.’ He does not know the words, does not understand their purport, but
only knows the shallow, near-at-hand, inferior dharma as a first step, greedily clinging to self and person, and forsaking the ultimate meaning.”
Shariputra, these people who do not
recognize the Dharma forsake the unsurpassed
treasure of the Dharma and fall
into wrong views; they are evil men among
shramanas (candalas). There are many
laypeople who go to them, and these
evil men preach the Dharma to those
laypeople. For the sake of fame and profit,
they praise the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Sangha. They but seek to sustain
their lives, become slaves to wealth
and property, greedily value clothing
and food, and praise what they themselves
delight in, saying: ‘If one
practices giving, one is reborn in heaven.’
Within the Buddha’s Dharma, giving is
an inferior dharma, yet they praise it
as the supreme dharma, and say: ‘Through
the cause of great giving one is
reborn in heaven.’ They do not know the
Buddha’s words, do not understand the
purport, but only know the shallow,
near-at-hand, inferior dharma as a first
step, greedily clinging to self and
person, forsaking the ultimate meaning.

[Chandala] The Chinese meaning is a dangerous evil person, one outside the four castes, who makes his living by slaughter. [Four castes] refers to the four social classes of ancient India: the Brahmans, the Kshatriyas, the Vaishyas, and the Shudras.

“Shariputra, preaching thus, at times some people give rise to faith and go forth from home, and unite together with these evil men, unable to diligently seek the ultimate profound meaning. Those who have something attained speak of a self, a person, a

living being, a soul, and remember and discriminate the dharmas that have no existence; within the Abhidharma and the sutras they form their own arguments, speaking now of annihilationism and eternalism, now of existence made, now of existence unmade.”
Shariputra, preaching thus, at times laypeople give rise to
faith and go forth from home, and unite together with these evil
men, unable to diligently seek the ultimate profound meaning.
They are those who have something attained, who speak of
a self, a person, a living being, a soul, and who remember and
discriminate dharmas that have no existence; within the
scriptures and treatises, not relying on the Buddha’s words, they
make up their own system, speaking now of annihilationism
and eternalism, now of existence made, now of existence unmade.
[Abhidharma] — the treatise. [Sutra] — that is
the sutra; here it refers to the scriptures.
“Shariputra, at that time my Dharma will contain many non-Buddhist dharmas, causing the mind of right view in all beings to be destroyed. Thus, Shariputra, my pure Dharma, because of this causal
condition, will gradually be extinguished. Shariputra, the bodhi that I long dwelt in birth-and-death and underwent all suffering to accomplish—that these evil men will destroy at that time.”

Shariputra, at that time the Buddha’s Dharma will be filled with non-Buddhist dharmas, causing the mind of right view in all beings to be misled into wrong views. Thus, Shariputra, my pure Dharma, because of this causal condition, will gradually be extinguished. Shariputra, the bodhi path that I, over a long time within birth and death, underwent all suffering to accomplish—is destroyed by these evil men at that time.

“Shariputra, if a bhikshu is unable to abandon the view of something attained, the view of self, the view of person, and does not understand what the Tathagata said as a skillful means, but declares that self and person truly exist, then I do not let such a man receive so much as

a single drink of water. Or, if such a man at times hears the Dharma of emptiness, his mind of faith is pure and he is not startled or doubtful, then he should in turn guide the multitude into the meaning of reality, and should go forth from home and receive the full precepts.”
Shariputra, if a bhikshu is unable to abandon the view of something attained, the view
of self, the view of person, and does not understand that this is the Tathagata’s
skillful-means speech, but declares that the dharma of self and person truly exists, then
I do not permit such people to receive even the offering of a single drink of water.
And if such a man at times hears the Dharma of emptiness, and his mind of faith is pure
and he is not startled or doubtful, then he should guide the multitude into the meaning
of reality, and such a man should go forth from home and receive the full precepts.
[Full precepts] the complete and perfect precepts, such as the two hundred and fifty
precepts of a bhikshu and the three hundred and forty-eight precepts of a bhikshuni.
“Why is that? Shariputra, if a man does not abandon such views, he is called
an outsider. Shariputra, by the causal condition of the conventional world I
provisionally speak of a self, but this is not the ultimate meaning. If a man
says: ‘I too, by the causal condition of the conventional world, speak of a
self’—if that man is able to understand the dharma that is unborn, undying, and
signless, and it does not contradict what I have said, then he is my disciple.”
Why is that? Shariputra, if a man does not abandon
such a view of something attained, the view
of self, the view of person, he is called an
outsider. Shariputra, by the causal condition of the
conventional world I provisionally speak of a
self, but this is not the ultimate meaning. If
a man says: ‘I too, by the causal condition of
the conventional world, speak of a self’—if that
man is able to understand the dharma that is
unborn, undying, and signless, and it does not
contradict what I have said, then he is my disciple.
“Shariputra, if a man says: ‘Why does the Tathagata, following worldly causal conditions, speak
of a person in the dharma of non-self? The Tathagata should not speak untrue words for the sake
of the world. Moreover, in many scriptures a person is spoken of, so what the Buddha says should
not be empty (false).’ Shariputra, one should answer such a man: The Buddha says all dharmas are
empty, without a master, without nature, but that which is merely false is not the ultimate
meaning. The Tathagata does not, for the sake of the ultimate meaning, speak of a self or a person.”
Shariputra, if a man says: ‘Why
does the Tathagata, following
worldly causal conditions,
speak of a self and a person
in the dharma of non-self?
The Tathagata should not, for
the sake of the world, speak
untrue words. Moreover, many
scriptures speak of a self
and a person, so what the Buddha
says should not be false.’
Shariputra, one should answer
such a man: ‘The Buddha says,
“all dharmas are empty,
without master, without nature”
— this is the ultimate truth;
“many scriptures speak of a
self” — this is the Buddha,
by worldly causal conditions,
provisionally speaking of a
self and a person; this is not
the ultimate meaning, but is
the conventional truth. The
Tathagata does not, for the
sake of the ultimate meaning,
speak of a self or a person.’

[The two truths] the conventional truth and the ultimate truth. The conventional truth is also called the worldly truth or the worldly-conventional truth, that is, the worldly phenomena seen by ordinary people; the ultimate truth is also called the truth of the ultimate meaning, or the supreme truth, that is, the real principle seen by the noble wisdom, namely the ineffable Dharmata realized inwardly.
“The speech of sages is without any greed or clinging; no man without wisdom is equal to the Buddha, nor is there any who surpasses him. Shariputra, the Tathagata’s
wisdom is inconceivable, and with this wisdom he knows the minds of beings. How could there be anyone equal to the Buddha? The Buddha is the great dragon, the king of
the great Dharma; one should not challenge him saying the Buddha speaks of a person. All the world constantly contends with me, but I never contend with the world.”
The speech of sages is without any
greed or clinging; it is impossible
for a man without wisdom to be
equal to the Buddha, nor is there
any who surpasses him. Shariputra,
the Tathagata’s wisdom is
inconceivable, and with this wisdom he
knows the minds of beings. Could
there be anyone equal to the Buddha?
The Buddha is the great dragon,
the king of the great Dharma; one
should not challenge him saying the
Buddha speaks of a self and a
person. All the world constantly
disputes with me, and I never dispute
with the world (because the
Tathagata knows truly that all dharmas
are neither taken up nor rejected,
neither disputed nor litigated).
[Ningdang (how could)]
— could it be that; how
could. [Zheng (contend)]
— contention, argument.
“Shariputra, those who speak of a self are deeply to be pitied. Herein there is neither a dharma
nor a self; many beings do not understand the Tathagata’s skillful-means speech, oppose the
treasure of the Dharma, and fall often into evil destinies. Shariputra, I know the wrong view yet I
do not hold the wrong view; one who is able to know the wrong view is precisely one of right
view. Shariputra, a wrong view never turns into a right view; the seeing does not know the seeing.”
Shariputra, those who speak of
a self are deeply to be pitied.
Within this ultimate meaning
there is neither a dharma nor a
self; many beings do not understand
that the Tathagata’s saying
‘there is a dharma, there is a
self’ is a skillful-means speech,
and so they oppose the treasure
of the Dharma and often fall
into evil paths. Shariputra, I
know the wrong view yet I do not
hold the wrong view; one who is
able to know the wrong view is
precisely one of right view.
Shariputra, a wrong view never
becomes a right view, and one of
wrong view is unable to know of
itself that it is a wrong view.
“Shariputra, the anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of the
Buddhas, the Tathagatas, is hard for all the world to
believe. Among all the devas and in all the world,
I am the most believable; I am not unbelievable.”
Shariputra, the anuttara-samyak-sambodhi
of the Buddhas,
the Tathagatas, is hard for all
the world to believe. Among
all the devas and in all the
world, I am the most trustworthy;
I am not untrustworthy.

“Shariputra, what I preach is for reaching the other shore, but therein there is no one who reaches the other shore; what I preach is for exhausting all conditioned actions, but therein there is no one who exhausts all conditioned actions; what I preach is for the sake of stilling, but therein there is no one who stills; what I preach is for the sake of parinirvana,

but therein there is no one who attains parinirvana; what I preach is for the sake of liberation, but therein there is no one who is liberated; what I preach is for the sake of all wisdoms, but therein there is no one who possesses all wisdoms; what I preach is for the sake of purifying defilements, but therein there is no one who purifies defilements.”
Shariputra, what I preach
is for reaching the
other shore of nirvana, but
within this ultimate
meaning there is no one
who reaches the other shore
of nirvana; what I
preach is for exhausting
all conditioned actions,
but within this ultimate
meaning there is no one
who exhausts all conditioned
actions; what I preach
is for the sake of
stilling, but within this
ultimate meaning there
is no one who stills; what
I preach is for the
sake of parinirvana, but
within this ultimate
meaning there is no one who
attains parinirvana; what
I preach is for the
sake of liberation, but
within this ultimate meaning
there is no one who is
liberated; what I preach
is for the sake of all
wisdoms, but within this
ultimate meaning there
is no one who possesses
all wisdoms; what I
preach is for the sake of
purifying defilements,
but within this ultimate
meaning there is no one
who purifies defilements.
[Parinirvana] that is nirvana.
“Extinction” is the extinguishing
of the three kinds of
delusion—views and thought,
dust-sand, and ignorance;
“crossing over” is the crossing
beyond the two kinds of
birth-and-death—that of delimited
bodies and that of transformation.
[All wisdoms] the various
deep wisdoms that clearly
understand the nature of things.

“Shariputra, the Tathagata preaches the Dharma for the devas, yet therein there are no devas; he preaches the Dharma for men, yet therein there are no men; he preaches the Dharma for beings, yet therein there are no beings. Shariputra, the Tathagata’s clear knowing and liberation—therein there is neither clear knowing nor liberation. I speak of recollection of the Buddha, but the Buddha is not to be recollected; I speak of the practice of emptiness, but emptiness is not to be practiced, nor is it to be recollected. Shariputra, this is called the phrases and verses of the Dharma that the Tathagata preaches, and therein there is no speaker. These evil men, obtaining these phrases and verses, preach them to others, and also take me as their teacher, yet without the merit of the Tathagata’s noble assembly, they still count themselves among the Sangha.”
Shariputra, the Tathagata preaches the Dharma to
the devas, yet there are no devas; he preaches
the Dharma to the assemblies of men, yet there
are no assemblies of men; he preaches the Dharma
to beings, yet there are no beings. Shariputra,
within this ultimate meaning the Tathagata’s
clear knowing and liberation—therein there is neither
clear knowing nor liberation. I speak of
recollection of the Buddha, but the Buddha is not to
be recollected; I speak of the practice of
emptiness, but emptiness is not to be practiced,
nor is it to be recollected. Shariputra, this is
what is called the phrases and verses of the Dharma
the Tathagata preaches, and therein there is
no speaker. These evil men, obtaining these
phrases and verses, preach them for others, and also
take me as their teacher, though having none of
the merit of the Tathagata’s noble assembly,
they yet think themselves to be among the Sangha.
[Clear knowing] a name for wisdom.
“Shariputra, just as a troop of monkeys is not like the Trayastrimsha heaven, in the same way these evil men are not like my noble assembly. Shariputra, these
evil men, merely by sound and speech, call themselves shramanas, just like the deluded man who saw a troop of monkeys and called it the Trayastrimsha heaven.”
Shariputra, just as a troop of monkeys is not like the heavenly princes of Trayastrimsha, in the same way these evil men
are not like my noble assembly. Shariputra, these evil men, merely by sound and speech, declare themselves to be
shramanas, just like the deluded man who saw a troop of monkeys and declared it to be the heavenly princes of Trayastrimsha.

“Shariputra, among them are renunciants who delight in asking and challenging; if they encounter a good teacher who preaches to them the stilling of name-and-form, the cutting off of the path of speech, the non-arising and non-waning, and the penetration of

the signless; and who, hearing such a Dharma of the unborn, the undying, the signless, is not startled or fearful—then know that such a man has already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, is able to know my Dharma, and may be called the noble assembly.”
Shariputra, among them are renunciants who delight in questioning and
debate; if they meet a good teacher who preaches to them the stilling of
name-and-form, the cutting off of the path of speech, the non-arising and
non-waning, and the penetration of the signless; and who, hearing such a
Dharma of the unborn, the undying, the signless, is not startled or
fearful—then know that such a man has already made offerings to immeasurable
Buddhas, is able to know my Dharma, and may be called the noble assembly.
[Name-and-form] the general name for the five aggregates. Within the
five aggregates, the four aggregates of feeling, perception,
volition, and consciousness are name, and the aggregate of form is form.
In this chapter, the World-Honored One reveals what impure Dharma-preaching is, and the dreadfulness of impure Dharma-preaching.
“The Buddha said to Shariputra: In the past, Kashyapa Buddha predicted of me, saying, ‘Because
Śākyamuni Buddha receives many offerings, the Dharma will swiftly be extinguished.’
Shariputra, my Dharma truly, because of many offerings, will later swiftly be extinguished.”

The Buddha said to Shariputra: In former times, when the Buddha Kashyapa made his prediction about me, he said: Because Śākyamuni Buddha receives many offerings, the Dharma will swiftly be extinguished. Shariputra, my Dharma truly, because of many offerings, will later swiftly be extinguished.

[Kashyapa Buddha] the Buddha immediately before Śākyamuni Buddha, one of the seven Buddhas. [Seven Buddhas] In the great eon (the Bhadrakalpa) where we now dwell, seven Buddhas have appeared: Vipashyin Buddha, Shikhin Buddha, Vishvabhu Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kashyapa Buddha, and Śākyamuni Buddha.

“Shariputra, for example, a poor man who obtains a great treasure is then greatly joyful. In the same way, Shariputra, in the future there will be many bhikshus who draw near to laypeople, receive their offerings, gradually become familiar with them and render them service, and their hearts are then delighted, taking this as joy and pleasure, just like a poor man who obtained a great treasure. Such deluded people value the slave of worldly profit and worldly pleasure. If they see a bhikshu with many offerings, they think in their hearts that he has attained arhatship; if they see one with few acquaintances, they call him an evil man. Such bhikshus, for the sake of profit and support, forsake the supreme Buddha path, and whatever they delight in they make their business.”

Shariputra, for example, a poor man who obtains a great treasure is then greatly joyful. In the same way, Shariputra, in the future there will be many bhikshus who draw near to laypeople (white-robed ones), receive their offerings, gradually become familiar with them and act as their servants (catering to them), and their hearts are then delighted at these offerings, taking them as joy and pleasure, just like a poor man who obtained a great treasure. Such deluded people are, with their whole hearts, willing to be slaves for worldly fame and worldly pleasures. If people see a bhikshu with many offerings, they think in their hearts that he is one who has attained arhatship, while seeing a bhikshu with few offerings, they think he is an evil man. These bhikshus who covet worldly profit and worldly pleasure, for the sake of gaining many offerings, forsake the supreme Buddha path, and preach the scriptures according to the tastes of the laypeople.
[And render them service] By the monastic rule, a bhikshu may not act as a servant to a layperson; he should transform them through the Dharma, and live purely by his own means.
“Shariputra, the Tathagata now speaks such scriptures as these for these deluded men. Why is that? A bhikshu who has broken the precepts, hearing this scripture, gives
rise to a mind of remorse and should return to keeping the precepts, not acting as a great thief receiving others’ offerings. Shariputra, if a bhikshu, hearing this
scripture, has a mind not pure, is neither pleased nor joyful—he is then called a corrupt and evil bhikshu. Why is that? Shariputra, a bhikshu of pure precepts is pleased
by no dharma without exception; whether one speaks of giving, whether one speaks of keeping the precepts, whether one speaks of patience, whether one speaks of vigor,
whether one speaks of meditation concentration, whether one speaks of wisdom, whether one speaks of such repugnant scriptures—his mind is rejoiced in all of them.”

Shariputra, the Tathagata now speaks this scripture (the Buddha Treasury scripture) for these deluded men. Why is that? A bhikshu who has broken the precepts, hearing this scripture, gives rise to a mind of remorse and returns to keeping the precepts, not acting as a great thief receiving their offerings. Shariputra, if a bhikshu, hearing this scripture, has a mind that is not pure, is neither pleased nor joyful, he is then called a corrupt and evil bhikshu. Why is that? Shariputra, a bhikshu of pure precepts, hearing this scripture, is pleased by no dharma without exception (because he deeply experiences the compassion of the World-Honored One in saving them, feeling the Buddha’s compassion and great kindness); whether one speaks of giving, of keeping the precepts, of patience, of vigor, of meditation concentration, of wisdom, or of such scriptures as make corrupt and evil bhikshus loathe and fear—in their hearts they are all greatly rejoiced.

“Shariputra, there are three kinds of people who, hearing this scripture, have minds that become distressed. Which three? First, a bhikshu who has broken the precepts; second, a man of overweening pride; third, one who preaches the Dharma impurely. And there are three further kinds of people who, hearing such a scripture, have minds that become distressed. Which three? First, the view of person; second, the view of a life; third, the view of self.”

Shariputra, there are three kinds of people who, hearing this scripture (the Buddha Treasury scripture), have minds that become distressed. Which three kinds? First, a bhikshu who has broken the precepts; second, a man of overweening pride; third, one who preaches the Dharma impurely. And there are three more kinds of people who, hearing such a scripture, have minds that become distressed. Which three kinds? First, one who has the view of a person; second, one who has the view of a life; third, one who has the view of a self.
[Śāriputra, I now clearly tell you: as a good spiritual friend, with a compassionate mind, one seeks benefit, joy, and security for others
(the same as “secure”)
; you should single-mindedly listen to and receive my words, always seeking the good benefit, and never be indolent.]

Śāriputra, I now clearly tell you that one should act as a good spiritual friend, and with a compassionate heart seek benefit, joy, and security for others. You should single-mindedly listen to and receive my words, always seeking the good benefit and never letting the mind be indolent.

[Śāriputra, one who impurely preaches the Dharma has five faults. What are the five? First, he claims himself to have fully known the Buddha Dharma; second, when preaching the Buddhist scriptures, he brings up the fault that the scriptures contradict one another; third, in his mind he doubts and does not believe the dharmas; fourth, with his own knowledge he condemns the Dharma of other scriptures; fifth, for the sake of profit and offerings he preaches the Dharma for others. Śāriputra, I say that such a person will fall into hell and will not reach nirvāṇa.]

Śāriputra, one who impurely preaches the Dharma has five faults. What are the five? First, he claims himself to have fully known the Buddha Dharma; second, when preaching the Buddhist scriptures, he points out the fault that the scriptures contradict one another (the Buddha preaches the Dharma through the two truths — the conventional and the ultimate; the impure preacher, knowing only how to grasp at appearances and not comprehending their meaning, actually declares the scriptures to be contradictory); third, in his mind he doubts and does not believe the dharmas; fourth, with his own knowledge he rashly criticizes the teachings as erroneous; fifth, for the sake of profit and offerings he preaches the Dharma for others. Śāriputra, I say that such a person will fall into hell and will not reach nirvāṇa.

[Two truths] The conventional truth and the ultimate truth. The conventional truth is also called the worldly truth or the truth of mundane convention — that is, the worldly phenomena seen by ordinary beings. The ultimate truth is also called the foremost meaning truth, or the supreme meaning truth — that is, the real principle seen by the wisdom of the sages, namely the inexpressible Dharma-nature realized inwardly. The Great Perfection of Wisdom Treatise says: “In the Buddha Dharma there are two truths: first, the worldly truth; second, the foremost meaning truth. For the sake of the worldly truth, it is said that there are sentient beings; for the sake of the foremost meaning truth, it is said that sentient beings have no existence.”

[Moreover, Śāriputra, when a preaching bhikṣu is present in the great assembly, and those who believe and delight in the Dharma spread a high seat for him, he abandons the Buddha’s right Dharma and preaches the finely adorned words of the outsiders. This Dharma-treasure, which I for a long time sought with diligent effort and hardship, this evil person sets aside and does not preach. Rather, with the contradictory meanings in the scriptures, he mutually affirms and denies, not following the right Dharma; in the Dharma of the sages he is lofty and arrogant, preaching at will for the sake of profit and offerings.]

Moreover, Śāriputra, when a preaching bhikṣu is present in the great assembly, and those who believe and delight in the Buddha Dharma spread a high seat for him, he abandons the Buddha’s right Dharma and preaches the fallacious theories that the outsiders adorn with fine words. This Dharma-treasure, which I through long eons sought with diligent effort and hardship, this evil person sets aside and does not preach. Rather, taking the contradictory meanings in the scriptures, he censures them, not following the right Dharma; in the Dharma of the sages he is arrogant and self-important, preaching at will for the sake of profit and offerings.

[Adorned with fine words] The wrong doctrines of the outsiders dare not state their principle plainly, clearly, and directly; instead, sparing no effort and going round about, they dress it up in gorgeous, flowery language — what the common saying calls “winding round and round” — in order to attain a hidden intent that cannot be spoken of.

[Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma mixed with the meaning of the outsiders, any good bhikṣu who diligently seeks the path should rise from his seat and go. Why? Śāriputra, because a believing layman has spread a high seat for him, he ought not to preach the meaning of the outsiders; if he does not leave, he is not a good bhikṣu, nor is he called one who follows the Buddha’s teaching.]

Śāriputra, this bhikṣu preaches the Dharma mixed with the meaning of the outsiders; if in the assembly there is a good bhikṣu who diligently seeks the path, he should leave. Why? Śāriputra, because a believing layman has spread a high seat for the preacher, the preacher ought not to preach the meaning of the outsiders. Now he, in pursuit of fame and profit, caters to the believers and preaches at will; if the diligent seeker does not leave, he is not a good bhikṣu, nor is he one who follows the Buddha’s teaching.

[Śāriputra, it is very difficult to preach the Dharma. One who preaches thus, I say, is called an outsider, a disciple of the Nirgranthas, not a disciple of the Buddha. After this preacher’s life ends, he will be born in the path of the Nirgranthas. What is the path of the Nirgranthas? Wrong views are the path of the Nirgranthas. What are wrong views? They are the hell realm, the animal realm, and the hungry ghost realm.]

Śāriputra, it is very difficult to preach the right Dharma. One who preaches so at will, I say, is a disciple of the Nirgrantha outsiders and not a disciple of the Buddha. After this preacher’s life ends, he will be born in the path of the Nirgranthas. What is the path of the Nirgranthas? The path of wrong views is the path of the Nirgranthas. What is the path of wrong views? It is the hell realm, the animal realm, and the hungry ghost realm.
[Nirgrantha (niqianzi)] One of the six great outsiders; it is also commonly used as a general name for those who leave home among the outsiders.

[Why? Śāriputra, one who has not personally realized the Dharma yet sits on the high seat, who himself does not know yet teaches others, will certainly fall into hell. Śāriputra, such causes and conditions the Tathāgata fully knows. My disciples, through various gates, various causes and conditions, and various views, destroy my right Dharma. Śāriputra, if any sentient being hears this sutra — the foremost meaning emptiness, the Dharma of non-existence — and rejoices in mind, one should know that such a person is truly my disciple.]

Why? Śāriputra, one who has not personally realized the Dharma yet sits on the high seat and preaches the Dharma, who himself does not know the Dharma yet teaches the Dharma to others, will certainly fall into hell. Śāriputra, such causes and conditions the Tathāgata fully knows. My disciples, through various gates, various causes and conditions, and various views, destroy my right Dharma. Śāriputra, if any sentient being hears this sutra — the foremost meaning emptiness, the Dharma of non-existence — and rejoices in mind, one should know that such persons are truly my disciples.

[Foremost meaning emptiness] In the Great Parinirvāṇa Sutra the Buddha says: “All dharmas are false and illusory; the place where they cease is called the real, called the real mark, called the Dharma-realm, called ultimate wisdom, called the foremost meaning truth, called the foremost meaning emptiness.” [Foremost meaning truth] The supreme, perfect, and ultimate truth.

[Śāriputra, in a past age there were five hundred blind people walking along a road. They came to a great city, exhausted with hunger and thirst. They had one blind person remain outside to guard the goods, while the rest entered the city to beg for food and drink. Before long a deceiver came to the guard of the goods and said: “Hey! Why do you stay here alone?” He replied: “I have many companions who have entered the city to beg for food.” The deceiver said: “Do you not know? There is a great distribution of clothing, food, necklaces, flowers, incense, and various things that you can have as you wish. If you need them, I will take you there.” He replied: “Very well.” The deceiver then led the blind man a little way from his place and robbed him of all his goods.]

Śāriputra, in a past age there were five hundred blind people walking along a road. They came to a great city, exhausted with hunger and thirst, so they had one blind person remain outside the city to guard the luggage, while the rest entered the city to beg for food and drink. Before long a swindler came to the guard and said: “Hey! Why do you stay here alone?” The guard replied: “I have many companions; they have entered the city to beg for food.” The swindler said: “Do you not know? There they are making a great distribution of clothing, food, necklaces, flowers, incense, and various things that you can have as you wish. If you want to go, I will take you there.” The guard replied: “All right.” The swindler then led this blind man away from his place and robbed him of all his goods.

[The blind people begged for food and, having obtained it, returned. The deceiver again said to the blind people: “Did you encounter the giving of the great assembly?” They answered: “We did not.” The deceiver said: “You may place what you have obtained here; I will take you to the great assembly’s giving.” The blind people all left their goods together in one place and followed the deceiver. The deceiver brought all five hundred blind people to the edge of a great deep pit and said to them: “This ground is level and good, and there is a great assembly’s giving. You may each turn and walk east to receive others’ gifts.” Thereupon, all at once, they fell into the pit and died.]

The blind people who had entered the city to beg for food, having obtained it, returned. The swindler again said to them: “Did you encounter the giving of the great assembly?” They answered: “We did not.” The swindler said: “Place what you have obtained here; I will take you to the place of the great assembly’s giving.” The blind people all left their goods in one place and followed the swindler. The swindler brought these five hundred blind people to the edge of a great deep pit and said to them: “This ground is level and good, and here is the great assembly’s giving. Turn and walk east, and you will obtain the gifts that are given.” The blind people, acting as the swindler told them, all fell into the pit and died.

[Śāriputra, future bhikṣus will be fond of reading the outsiders’ scriptures; when they preach the Dharma they will embellish their words so as to make the assembly rejoice. At that time the evil Māra will assist them in deluding the multitude and obstructing the good Dharma. If there are those who greedily cling to sound, to speech, to cleverly adorned words, or even those who are fond of reading the outsiders’ scriptures, Māra will delude them all and make their minds secure and at ease. If there are bhikṣus who truly cultivate the Buddha Dharma, Māra causes the multitude to give rise to doubt toward them, so that they no longer make offerings to them. Or, if there are bhikṣus who have in some measure — two or three — already read the Buddha scriptures, Māra makes them seek the outsiders’ scriptures and teachings, praising them as good and excellent. These people, deluded by Māra, with the eye of wisdom covered and obstructed, deeply greedy for profit and offerings, read the various outside books, just like a flock of the blind deceived by a swindler, all made to fall into a deep pit and die.]

Śāriputra, future bhikṣus will be fond of reading the outsiders’ scriptures; when preaching the Dharma they will hide and adorn it with beautiful words, making the assembly rejoice. At that time the evil Māra assists him in deluding the multitude and obstructing the propagation of the good Dharma. If there are those who greedily cling to sound, to speech, and to cleverly adorned words, and who are also fond of reading the outsiders’ scriptures, Māra deludes them all and makes their minds secure and at ease. If there are bhikṣus who truly cultivate the Buddha Dharma, Māra causes the multitude to give rise to doubt toward them, so that they no longer make offerings to them. Or, if there are bhikṣus — two or three of them — who have already read the Buddha scriptures, Māra misleads them into seeking the outsiders’ scriptures and teachings, praising them as good and excellent. These people, deluded by Māra, with the eye of wisdom covered and obstructed, deeply greedy for profit and offerings, go to read the various outside books, just like a flock of the blind deceived by a swindler, falling into a deep pit and dying.

[Śāriputra, those born blind are the bhikṣus: they abandon the Buddha’s unsurpassed path and seek the outsiders’ scriptures. The swindler is the evil Māra; the deep pit is the wrong path. Śāriputra, just as the flock of the blind, abandoning what they had obtained, wished to go to the great giving and fell into a deep pit, so too my disciples, abandoning coarse clothing and food and chasing after the great giving to seek fine offerings, on account of worldly profit lose great wisdom and fall into the deep pit of the Avīci hell.]

Śāriputra, the born-blind who were deceived are those bhikṣus who abandon the Buddha’s unsurpassed path and pursue the outsiders’ scriptures. The swindler is the evil Māra; the deep pit is the wrong path. Śāriputra, just as the flock of the blind abandoned what they had obtained, vainly seeking to gain the great giving and so fell into a deep pit, so too my disciples, abandoning coarse clothing and food and pursuing the great giving to seek fine offerings, on account of worldly fame and profit lose great wisdom and fall into the deep pit of the Avīci hell.
[Born blind] One who is blind from birth.

[Moreover, Śāriputra, one who impurely preaches the Dharma does not know the Tathāgata’s adaptive and expedient intention, and not understanding it well himself, preaches for others. Such a person obtains five faults in this present life. Other people do not know them; only the bhikṣu who has obtained the divine eye and the gods know them. What are the five? First, when preaching the Dharma he is full of fear in his heart, afraid someone may challenge him. Second, inwardly distressed and fearful, he yet preaches for others. Third, he is an ordinary person without true wisdom. Fourth, what he preaches is impure, empty of anything but words. Fifth, his speech is without order, patching together extracts everywhere. For this reason, in the assembly, his heart is filled with terror.]

Moreover, Śāriputra, one who impurely preaches the Dharma does not know the Tathāgata’s adaptive intention, and not understanding it well himself, preaches rashly for others. Such a person obtains five faults in this present life. Other people do not know them; only the bhikṣu who has obtained the divine eye and the gods in heaven know them. What are the five faults? First, when preaching the Dharma he is full of fear in his heart, afraid someone may censure and refute him. Second, inwardly distressed and fearful, yet he preaches for others (not himself understanding the Buddha Dharma, yet wishing to proclaim it, so his heart is fearful). Third, he is an ordinary person without true wisdom. Fourth, what he preaches is impure — what he preaches is not the truth — but he expends his effort on fine, flowery words. Fifth, his speech is without order, rambling here and there (because he has not himself thoroughly comprehended it). For this reason, in the assembly, his heart is filled with terror.

[Not knowing the Tathāgata’s adaptive intention] The World-Honored One, in accord with the capacities of beings, spoke of the Two Vehicles and the Three Vehicles; these are expedient teachings, while the true teaching is the One Buddha Vehicle. The Lotus Sutra

Skillful Means chapter says: “In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions there is only the One Vehicle Dharma, with no second and no third, apart from the Buddha’s expedient preaching.” It also says: “Only this one thing is real; the other two are not true.” [Expedient and real] The teaching suitable for a time is called “expedient”; the ultimate and unchanging teaching is called “real.” [No second and no third, apart from the Buddha’s expedient preaching] There is no Two Vehicles and no Three Vehicles; the Two Vehicles and Three Vehicles are the Buddha’s expedient preaching. [Two Vehicles] The Śrāvaka vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha vehicle. [Three Vehicles] The Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Bodhisattva vehicle. The Śrāvaka vehicle is also called the lesser vehicle; the Pratyekabuddha vehicle is also called the middle vehicle; the Bodhisattva vehicle is also called the great vehicle.

[Such an ordinary person has no wisdom and no settled mind, but from the trivial causes of pride and the like seeks fame; with doubt and regret in his heart, he preaches for others. Such a person, in the long night, himself receives the poisoned arrows of greed, hatred, and delusion. Why? Śāriputra, this person cannot definitively know the dharmas, and preaches them for others; his mind is not joyful, and if he has any joy it is quickly lost. Śāriputra, I know that impure preaching has this fault, and that it does not attain the right path. This matter all the bhikṣus do not know, the gods do not know; I alone know it.]

Such an ordinary person has no wisdom, and in his mind has no settled faith and understanding, but from the trivial causes of pride, the pursuit of profit, and the like, seeks fame; with doubt and regret in his heart, he preaches the Dharma for others. These people, in the long night, themselves receive the poisoned arrows of greed, hatred, and delusion. Why? Śāriputra, these people cannot definitively know the dharmas, and yet preach them for others; while preaching, their own minds are not joyful, and even if they have a little joy it is quickly lost. Śāriputra, I know that impure preaching has this fault, and that it does not attain the right path. This matter all the bhikṣus do not know, the gods do not know; I alone know it.

[There is also impure preaching. A bhikṣu does not understand the Tathāgata’s adaptive preaching, and preaches for others. The scriptures speak of no self, no person, no sentient being, no life; but this person, with his own arguments, says: there is a self, there is a person, there is a sentient being, there is a life. This is slandering the Buddha, slandering the Dharma, and slandering the Saṅgha. The offense of slandering the Three Jewels the gods and people of the world cannot know; only the Buddha knows it. Śāriputra, this person is also called one who impurely preaches the Dharma. I know his fault; those with supernormal powers and the multitudes of gods all cannot know it; only the Buddha knows it.]

There is also impure preaching. A bhikṣu does not understand what the Tathāgata taught in accord with the capacities of beings, and relying on his own intention preaches rashly for others. The scriptures speak of no self, no person, no sentient being, no life; but this person, with his own arguments, says: there is a self, there is a person, there is a sentient being, there is a life. This is slandering the Buddha, slandering the Dharma, and slandering the Saṅgha. The terror of this offense of slandering the Three Jewels the gods and the people of the world cannot know; only the Buddha knows it. Śāriputra, this person is also called one who impurely preaches the Dharma. I know his fault; those with supernormal powers and the multitudes of gods all cannot know it; only the Buddha knows it.
[No self, no person, no sentient being, no life] Self, others, sentient beings, and life are all illusions and do not exist at all.

[Śāriputra, I will now explain to you by a parable. If a person who does not know the meaning and characteristics of the Buddha path impurely preaches the Dharma for others, how many unwholesome matters does this person accomplish? Śāriputra, what do you think — are the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa numerous or not? “Very numerous, World-Honored One.” Śāriputra, if an evil person took away the lives of them all, would the offense of this person be great? “Very great, World-Honored One.” Just so, this deluded person who does not know the Buddha path and impurely preaches the Dharma for others incurs a greater offense than this.]

Śāriputra, I will now explain by a parable the terror of the offense of impure preaching and slandering the Three Jewels: if a person who does not know the meaning and characteristics of the Buddha path impurely preaches the Dharma for others, this person accomplishes this dangerous and evil matter. Śāriputra, what do you think — are the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa not very numerous? Śāriputra replied: “Very numerous, World-Honored One.” The World-Honored One said: “Śāriputra, if an evil person killed all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, would the offense this person obtains not be very great?” Śāriputra replied: “Very great, World-Honored One.” The World-Honored One said: “Just so, such a deluded person who does not know the Buddha path and impurely preaches the Dharma for others incurs a greater offense than this.”

[How many unwholesome matters does this person accomplish] Here “how many” has the meaning of “dangerous.” The Mozi says: “What is not firm in its root will surely be endangered at its tip.” [Jambudvīpa] Also called the southern continent; in Chinese it is translated “the Victorious Gold Continent” — that is, the Sahā world in which we dwell, also called the southern Jambudvīpa.

[Why? Because this person, impurely preaching the Dharma, destroys the unsurpassed Buddha path and also slanders the past, future, and present Buddhas. Why? Śāriputra, if there are past Buddhas, they all say that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without a life, without a soul. Śāriputra, the future Buddhas also say that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without a life, without a soul. Śāriputra, the Buddhas now present in the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all say that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without a life, without a soul. Śāriputra, this is called the unsurpassed Dharma of the Buddhas: that all dharmas have no essence, the emptiness of non-attainment, their nature still and extinct, without arising and without ceasing, without nature and mark, their own marks all empty.]

Why? Because such a deluded person, impurely preaching the Dharma, destroys the unsurpassed Buddha path and also slanders the past, future, and present Buddhas. Why? Śāriputra, the past Buddhas all say that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without a life, without a soul. Śāriputra, the future Buddhas also all say that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without a life, without a soul. Śāriputra, the Buddhas now present in the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, also all say that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without a life, without a soul. Śāriputra, the unsurpassed Dharma of the Buddhas is this: that all dharmas have no essence, the emptiness of non-attainment, their nature still and extinct, without arising and without ceasing, without nature and mark, their own marks all empty.

[The Tathāgata speaks only for the sake of cutting off all recollections and discriminations; the Buddhas’ bodhi is without discrimination. Śāriputra, what is discrimination? What is called discrimination is the view of self, the view of person, the view of sentient being, the view of a life, the view of a soul, the annihilationist view, and the eternalist view; ordinary beings accomplish these discriminations. If a person has no such discriminations, and can fully know that all dharmas are empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without a life, without a soul, then when he thinks thus his mind rejoices, and hearing the foremost meaning emptiness he is not startled and not afraid. This person then knows the five aggregates are false and illusory, without reality; knows the twelve sense-entrances and the eighteen elements are false and illusory, without reality. This person also does not discriminate nirvāṇa, does not think of nirvāṇa, does not say “I can think of nirvāṇa and, through the Dharma, attain stillness”; he does not discriminate. As to where the Dharma is still and extinct, he does not discriminate, nor does he obtain it. Śāriputra, this is called compliance-endurance. This person, in this compliance-endurance within the foremost meaning, also does not obtain a self-mark.]

The Tathāgata speaks only for the sake of sentient beings, to cut off all recollections and discriminations; the Buddhas’ anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is without discrimination. Śāriputra, what is discrimination? What is called discrimination is the view of self, the view of person, the view of sentient being, the view of a life, the view of a soul, the annihilationist view, and the eternalist view; ordinary beings accomplish these discriminations. If a person has no such discriminations, he can fully know that all dharmas are empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without a life, without a soul. When he thinks thus his mind rejoices; hearing the foremost meaning emptiness he is not startled and not afraid. This person then knows the five aggregates are false and illusory, without reality; knows the twelve sense-entrances and the eighteen elements are false and illusory, without reality. This person also does not discriminate nirvāṇa, does not think of nirvāṇa, and does not say “I can think of nirvāṇa and, through the Dharma, attain stillness”; he does not discriminate. As to where the Dharma is still and extinct, he does not discriminate, nor does he obtain it. Śāriputra, this is called compliance-endurance. This person, in this compliance-endurance within the foremost meaning, also does not obtain a self-mark.

[Annihilationist view] The deluded clinging that after death the five aggregates, body and mind, all cease. [Eternalist view] The deluded clinging that this five-aggregate body and mind, though they cease in this life, are reborn in a future life, continuing without interruption, abiding forever without extinction.

[The five aggregates] The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. These five, being accumulated and arising, are called the “five aggregates”; and because they can cover over a person’s true nature, causing him to be deluded and inverted and to create various karmas, they are also called the “five shadows.” Among them, the aggregate of form refers to matter and is called the “dharma of form”; the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness belong to the mind and are called the “dharmas of mind.” These are the five great elements that constitute body and mind. Among them, the aggregate of form is the body; the other four aggregates (feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness) are the mind.

The Sutra of Complete Enlightenment says: “What is ignorance? Good man! All sentient beings, from time without beginning, have many kinds of inversion, just like a deluded person who takes the four directions to have changed places: they mistakenly take the four great elements as the form of the self, and the shadow-traces of the six sense-objects as the form of the mind. It is like one who has diseased eyes seeing flowers in the empty sky and a second moon. Good man! The sky truly has no flowers; the sick one deludedly clings to them. Because of this deluded clinging, not only is he confused about the nature of this empty sky, he is also confused about the place where the real flowers arise. From this illusion there is false existence, and he revolves in birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.”

[Śāriputra, what is the mark of compliance-endurance? That which is called signlessness is the mark of compliance-endurance. Śāriputra, what do you think — if a person in this compliance-endurance does not even obtain a mark, then if this person obtained the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, the mark of a life, or the mark of a soul, that would be impossible. If a person accomplishes such wisdom, he should receive offerings; he is called a son of the Buddha, called entering the concentration of non-abiding. Śāriputra, this is called the foremost meaning gate of the Buddha Dharma, meaning without recollection and discrimination, without this and without that. But this deluded person, in the great assembly preaching wrong views, teaching others with his own recollections and discriminations — “this is the Buddha Dharma, this is the holy path” — such a deluded person slanders the past, future, and present Buddhas. Such a deluded person is called an evil spiritual friend, not a good spiritual friend.]

Śāriputra, what is the mark of compliance-endurance? That which is called signlessness is the mark of compliance-endurance. Śāriputra, what do you think — if a person in this compliance-endurance does not even obtain a mark, then if this person obtained the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, the mark of a life, or the mark of a soul, that would be impossible. If a person accomplishes such wisdom, he should receive offerings; he is called a son of the Buddha, called entering the concentration of non-abiding. Śāriputra, this is called the foremost meaning gate of the Buddha Dharma, meaning without recollection and discrimination, without this and without that. But those deluded persons, in the great assembly preaching wrong views and teaching others with their own recollections and discriminations, saying “this is the Buddha Dharma, this is the holy path” — such deluded persons slander the past, future, and present Buddhas. Such deluded persons are called evil spiritual friends, not good spiritual friends.

[Śāriputra, an enemy, though he takes life, only causes the loss of one body. But such a deluded person, impurely preaching the Dharma, in thousands of millions of eons causes great decay and affliction to sentient beings. This person’s dark delusion covers the original mind of the Buddhas’ bodhi; his greed and clinging blaze up again and again, continuing without interruption. Because of greed and clinging, he goes back and forth among the five realms, with no good path, birth and death without end. Therefore, Śāriputra, one who impurely preaches the Dharma incurs very great offenses, and also serves as an evil spiritual friend to sentient beings, and also slanders the past, future, and present Buddhas.]

Śāriputra, a thieving enemy who takes life only causes the loss of one body. But such a deluded person, impurely preaching the Dharma, in thousands of millions of eons causes great decay and affliction to sentient beings. The darkness of this person’s delusion covers the Buddha-nature (the original mind of bodhi); his greed and clinging blaze up again and again, continuing without interruption. Because of greed and clinging, he goes back and forth among the five realms, and without the good path (the human and heavenly realms), birth and death have no end. Therefore, Śāriputra, one who impurely preaches the Dharma incurs very great offenses, also serves as an evil spiritual friend to sentient beings, and also slanders the past, future, and present Buddhas.
[The five realms] First, the hell realm; second, the hungry ghost realm; third, the animal realm; fourth, the human realm; fifth, the heavenly realm.

[Śāriputra, not to mention the sentient beings of this Jambudvīpa — if a person deprived all the sentient beings of the three-thousand great-thousand world of life, the offense of impure preaching is greater than this. Why? Because such a person destroys the Buddhas’ anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, assists the affairs of Māra, and causes sentient beings to undergo decay and affliction for hundreds of thousands of eons; he can only bind them and cannot release them. One should know that such a person is, toward sentient beings, an evil spiritual friend, one who speaks false words, and in the great assembly slanders the Buddhas; on account of these causes and conditions he falls into the great hell. He teaches many sentient beings the matter of wrong views; therefore he is called one of evil wrong views.]
Śāriputra, not to mention this taking away the lives of all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa,
if a person takes away the lives of all the sentient beings of the three-thousand great-thousand world, the offense of impure preaching is greater than this.

(Earlier it was said that the offense of impure preaching is greater than killing all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa; here it goes further, saying that the offense of impure preaching is greater than killing all the sentient beings of the three-thousand great-thousand world — a parable showing how terrifying impure preaching is!) Why does impure preaching carry such a heavy offense? Because these impure preachers all destroy the Buddhas’ anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and assist the affairs of Māra; they also cause sentient beings to undergo decay and affliction for hundreds of thousands of eons.
