They can only bind and cannot release. One should know that such persons are, toward sentient beings, evil spiritual friends, speaking false words, and in the great assembly slandering the Buddhas; on account of these causes and conditions they fall into the great hell. They teach many sentient beings the matter of wrong views; therefore they are called those of evil wrong views.

[Śāriputra, those with the view of self, the view of person, and the view of sentient being mostly fall into wrong views; those who eradicate these views quickly attain the path. Why? Because these are easy to abandon. For this reason, one should know that such a person would rather cut out his own tongue with a sharp knife than impurely preach the Dharma in the assembly.]

Śāriputra, those with the view of self, the view of person, and the view of sentient being mostly fall into wrong views; whereas those who have eradicated the view of self, the view of person, and the view of sentient being all quickly attain the path. Why? Because those who have eradicated the view of self, the view of person, and the view of sentient being find them easy to abandon (leaving the marks, not clinging to marks). For this reason, one should know that such deluded persons would rather cut off their own tongues with a sharp knife than impurely preach the Dharma in the assembly.

blocks.text: The Chapter on the Past, the Seventh

inline.s: In this chapter, the World-Honored One holds up the past as a mirror for the present, explaining the great retribution of impure preaching and the long eons in which its followers fall into hell; while “if a person wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and preaches the Dharma for others, he obtains immeasurable and boundless merit, and is also able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.”
[The Buddha told Śāriputra: In the past, in a distant, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable asamkhyeya eon, at that time there was a Buddha named the Tathāgata of Great Adornment, the Worthy
(the text here omits one character — “gòng,” meaning “offerings”)

, the Fully Awakened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone One, knower of the world, the supreme being, the tamer of men, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.]

Śākyamuni Buddha instructed Śāriputra, saying: In the past, in a distant, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable asamkhyeya eon, at that time there was a Buddha named the Tathāgata of Great Adornment, the Worthy One, the Fully Awakened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone One, knower of the world, the supreme being, the tamer of men, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

[Asamkhyeya] That is, asamkhyeya; in Chinese it is translated “countless,” meaning so many that no number can count them. [The Tathāgata’s titles] The Tathāgata has the following honorific titles: First, the Tathāgata — one who, by the path of suchness, comes and attains right enlightenment. Second, the Worthy One — worthy of the offerings of humans and gods. Third, the Fully Awakened One — truly and universally knowing all dharmas. Fourth, perfect in knowledge and conduct — possessing the three insights of the insight into past lives, the divine eye, and the insight into the extinction of outflows, together with the five conducts of holy conduct, brahma conduct, heavenly conduct, infant conduct, and sick conduct, all complete. Fifth, the Well-Gone One — freely and well gone, entering nirvāṇa. Sixth, knower of the world — able to understand the principle of all worldly matters. Seventh, the supreme being — the one supreme and unrivaled. Eighth, the tamer of men — the great man who can tame and guide beings to the right path. Ninth, the teacher of gods and humans — the Buddha is the teacher of all gods and humans. Tenth, the Buddha — in Sanskrit the full title is “Buddha”; in Chinese “the Awakened One,” meaning wisdom fully complete and the three enlightenments consummated (self-enlightenment, enlightening others, and enlightenment-and-practice consummated), knowing and seeing all dharmas of the three times. Eleventh, the World-Honored One — the Buddha is the one whom all the people of the world jointly revere.

[That Buddha’s lifespan was sixty-eight hundred million nayuta years, and he had sixty-eight hundred million nayuta great disciples. After that Buddha passed into extinction, his relics were distributed everywhere, exactly as after my extinction. His right Dharma also abided in the world for five hundred years, exactly as after my extinction.]

The Tathāgata of Great Adornment’s lifespan was sixty-eight hundred million nayuta years, and he had sixty-eight hundred million nayuta great disciples. After the Tathāgata of Great Adornment passed into extinction, his relics were distributed throughout the four quarters, exactly the same as after my extinction. The right Dharma of the Tathāgata of Great Adornment also abided in the world for five hundred years, exactly the same as after my extinction.

[After that Buddha passed into extinction, among his great disciples, in one day there were a hundred bhikṣus who entered nirvāṇa; two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, five hundred entered nirvāṇa; in one day there might even be a hundred thousand nayuta bhikṣus entering nirvāṇa. Thus in turn, all of that Buddha’s greatly wise, greatly learned, and greatly supernaturally powerful assembly entered nirvāṇa within three months.]

After the Tathāgata of Great Adornment passed into extinction, among his great disciples, in one day there were a hundred bhikṣus entering nirvāṇa; in one day there were two hundred bhikṣus entering nirvāṇa; in one day there were three hundred bhikṣus entering nirvāṇa; in one day there were four hundred bhikṣus entering nirvāṇa; in one day there were five hundred bhikṣus entering nirvāṇa; and even in one day there might be a hundred thousand nayuta bhikṣus entering nirvāṇa. Thus in turn, all of that Buddha’s greatly wise, greatly learned, and greatly supernaturally powerful assembly entered nirvāṇa one after another within three months.
[All successively entered nirvāṇa] Because the great disciples had all realized the fruit of arhat, coming and going freely, they themselves could decide when to enter nirvāṇa.

[Śāriputra, the right Dharma of the Buddha of Great Adornment spread abroad, and many gods and people together made offerings to it. Śāriputra, after the Buddha of Great Adornment and his great disciples passed into extinction, gradually many people came to know that the Dharma of the śramaṇas is secure and joyful, and left home to study the path, but they could not understand the unequaled meaning of emptiness of the profound sutras preached by the Buddha, and were mostly deluded by the evil Māra. At that time, the preachers’ minds were not settled, and their preaching was impure; they spoke of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life, and did not speak of all dharmas as empty and still.]

Śāriputra, the right Dharma of the Buddha of Great Adornment spread abroad, and very many hosts of gods and people together made offerings to it. Śāriputra, after the Buddha of Great Adornment and his great disciples passed into extinction, gradually many people came to know that the Dharma of the śramaṇas is secure and happy, and so left home to study the path; yet they could not understand the unequaled meaning of emptiness of the profound sutras spoken by the Buddha (because the great disciples of the Tathāgata of Great Adornment had all entered nirvāṇa), and were mostly deluded by the evil Māra. At that time, the preachers had no settled faith in the Buddha’s right Dharma (no unshakable, single-minded faith free of doubt); most preached impurely, deludedly clinging to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life as really existing, and did not speak of all dharmas as empty and still.
[Secure (anyin)] That is, “secure and at ease.”

[Having a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life] This is what the Diamond Sutra calls the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, and the mark of a life. The Buddha said: “If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, and the mark of a life, he is not a bodhisattva.” [The mark of self] Deludedly clinging to the five-aggregate body and mind as real, and taking it as “self” and giving rise to the mind — for example, gain and loss, favorable and adverse, honor and disgrace, and so on. [The mark of person] Deludedly clinging to the other party, to other people, as really existing and giving rise to the mind — for example, love and hate, right and wrong, high and low, and so on. [The mark of sentient being] Here “sentient beings” refers to groups of people, for example groups distinguished by closeness and distance, likes and dislikes, friend and enemy, age, sex, work unit, region, ethnicity, skin color, country, and so on. The mark of sentient being is deludedly clinging to these groups of people as real and giving rise to a discriminative mind. [The mark of a life] Deludedly clinging to a life-span as real and reckoning its length or shortness. Of all the things the deluded sentient beings care about most, there is nothing more than a life-span; therefore the mark of a life is separated out from the mark of self and set up as its own item.

[After that Buddha had passed into extinction a hundred years, the assembly of disciples divided into five groups: the first named Pushi, the second named Ku’an, the third named Saheduo, the fourth named Jiangqu, and the fifth named Bannantu. Śāriputra, these five bhikṣus — Pushi, Ku’an, Saheduo, Jiangqu, and Bannantu — were the teachers of the great assembly. The one named Pushi knew the real meaning of emptiness as spoken by the Buddha, the Dharma of non-attainment; the other four bhikṣus all followed wrong paths, speaking much of a self and speaking much of a person.]

After the Tathāgata of Great Adornment had passed into extinction a hundred years, the assembly of disciples divided into five groups: the first named Pushi, the second named Ku’an, the third named Saheduo, the fourth named Jiangqu, and the fifth named Bannantu. Śāriputra, these five — the bhikṣu Pushi, the bhikṣu Ku’an, the bhikṣu Saheduo, the bhikṣu Jiangqu, and the bhikṣu Bannantu — became the teachers of the great assembly. The bhikṣu Pushi knew the real meaning of emptiness as spoken by the Buddha, the Dharma of non-attainment; the other four bhikṣus all fell into wrong paths, speaking of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life.

[Śāriputra, the bhikṣu Pushi was despised by the four groups, had no power or influence, and was much hated and disdained. The four evil bhikṣus taught the multitudes many wrong views; being irreverent and defiant toward the Buddha’s Dharma, they thereby destroyed the Dharma.]

Śāriputra, the group of the bhikṣu Pushi was slighted by the other four groups, had no power or influence, and (under the powerful influence of the four evil bhikṣus) was much hated and disdained. The four evil bhikṣus — Ku’an, Saheduo, Jiangqu, and Bannantu — taught the multitudes many paths of wrong views, showing no reverence for and not following the Buddha’s Dharma; they went against the Dharma and thereby destroyed it.

[Śāriputra, if a person knows the Dharma of emptiness spoken by the bhikṣu Pushi and believes and accepts it without resistance, I know that this person has in a former life made offerings to five thousand Buddhas, and that sixty-eight hundred million nayuta persons have already entered nirvāṇa. Why? Śāriputra, these persons planted many good roots at the place of the Buddhas in past lives, cultivated the non-attaining Dharma of emptiness, and were due to enter nirvāṇa.]

Śāriputra, if a person knows the Dharma of emptiness spoken by the bhikṣu Pushi and believes and accepts it without resistance, I know that this person has, in a former life, made offerings to five thousand Buddhas, and that of such persons sixty-eight hundred million nayuta have already entered nirvāṇa. Why? Śāriputra, these persons planted many good roots at the place of the Buddhas in past lives, cultivated the non-attaining Dharma of emptiness, and were due to enter nirvāṇa.
[Nayuta] It is equivalent to the number we call a hundred million today; there are also those who say it is a hundred billion.

[Śāriputra, the bhikṣu Ku’an, the bhikṣu of all existence, the bhikṣu Jiangqu, and the bhikṣu Bannantu all calculated attainment, speaking of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life, and their assemblies flourished. These four evil persons caused many, both lay and monastic, to abide in wrong views, abandoning the foremost meaning, the Dharma of non-attainment, the ultimately-empty Dharma, and delighting in the treatises of the Nirgrantha heretics. Śāriputra, the lay and monastic disciples of these four evil persons followed them constantly, even to the end of the Dharma.]

Śāriputra, these four evil bhikṣus (the bhikṣu Ku’an, the bhikṣu Saheduo, the bhikṣu Jiangqu, and the bhikṣu Bannantu) all calculated and clung to attainment, speaking of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life; because they catered to what the world liked, their assemblies flourished. These four evil persons caused many, both lay and monastic, to abide in wrong views, abandoning the foremost meaning, the Dharma of non-attainment, the ultimately-empty Dharma, and delighting in the treatises of heretics. Śāriputra, the lay and monastic disciples of these four evil persons followed them constantly, even to the extinction of the Dharma.
[The bhikṣu of all existence] This refers to the bhikṣu Saheduo.

[Śāriputra, among them, if a person knows something to be non-Dharma but receives it as Dharma and diligently practices it, they still cannot obtain compliance-endurance, much less the fruit of stream-entry! Such a person cannot even consummately receive offerings, much less give rise to compliance-endurance!]

Śāriputra, among the lay and monastic disciples of the four evil persons, there are those who hear their non-Dharma wrong teachings and mistakenly take them as true Dharma, and so diligently practice them. These persons who mistakenly believe in the wrong teachings cannot even obtain compliance-endurance, much less attain the fruit of stream-entry! Such persons cannot even consummately receive offerings, much less give rise to compliance-endurance!

[Compliance-endurance] That is, compliance-endurance, the endurant compliance with the Dharma spoken of in the preceding passage. [Stream-entry] The first fruit among the four fruits of the Śrāvaka vehicle. [Four fruits] The four stages of the Śrāvaka vehicle: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returner, the fruit of non-returner, and the fruit of arhat.

[Śāriputra, at that time the lay and monastic disciples mostly fell into evil destinies and did not reach the good destinies. These evil persons destroyed the Buddha’s true Dharma and also brought great sorrow and distress to many.]

Śāriputra, at that time the lay and monastic disciples of the four evil bhikṣus, one after another, fell into evil destinies and did not reach the good destinies. These evil persons destroyed the Buddha’s true Dharma and also caused many who followed them to suffer great hardship.

[Moreover, after these evil persons died, they fell into the Avīci hell, lying on their backs for nine hundred million trillion years, lying on their faces for nine hundred million trillion years, lying on their left side for nine hundred million trillion years, and lying on their right side for nine hundred million trillion years on the hot iron, burned and scorched within it. When they died there they were born again into the scorching hell, the great scorching hell, the living hell, and the black-cord hell, all experiencing such suffering for the same numbers of years. Dying in the black-cord hell, they were born again into the great Avīci hell.]

Moreover, after these evil persons died, they fell into the Avīci hell, lying on their backs on the hot iron for nine hundred million trillion years, lying on their faces for nine hundred million trillion years, lying on their left side for nine hundred million trillion years, and lying on their right side for nine hundred million trillion years, burned and scorched within the Avīci hell. After dying in the Avīci hell, they were born into the scorching hell, the great scorching hell, the living hell, and the black-cord hell, in each experiencing the various torments of lying on their backs, on their faces, on their left side, and on their right side for nine hundred million trillion years. Finally, dying in the black-cord hell, they were born again into the great Avīci hell to continue suffering.
[Scorched (jiao)] An ancient word, the same as “jiao” (charred).
[Śāriputra, for this reason, if lay or monastic persons befriend this person, and good friends
(excellent acquaintances)
and all the donors, in all six hundred and four trillion people, were born and died together with these four teachers, experiencing all the burning and boiling in the great hell.]

Śāriputra, for this reason, all who, lay or monastic, befriend these four evil bhikṣus, along with their close friends (good acquaintances) and donors (dānapati), in all six hundred and four trillion people, shared life and death with the four evil bhikṣus, fell together into hell, and all experienced every manner of burning and boiling in the great hell.

[Thus, Śāriputra, all the families of kind friends, the families of donors, the disciples, the teachers, and those who followed along — all within that number — were born in hell. Śāriputra, you cannot know how many they are; only the Tathāgata can know. Those who fell into the great hell with these evil persons, born and dying together, in all six hundred and four trillion people, thus turned and suffered through a kalpa. Because the great kalpa was about to burn, they were in hell. Why? Śāriputra, to destroy the Tathāgatas’ anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is a very heavy offense, not a light one.]

Thus, Śāriputra, all the supporters of the four evil bhikṣus, the families of all the donors (dānapati), the disciples, the teachers, and those who followed along — all within that number — were born in hell. Śāriputra, you cannot know how many there are; only the Tathāgata can know. Those who, together with the four evil bhikṣus, fell into the great hell, born and dying together, in all six hundred and four trillion people, thus turned and suffered through a great kalpa. They remained in hell suffering until just before the kalpa-fire was about to burn. Why? Śāriputra, they destroyed the Tathāgatas’ anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; their offense is very heavy, not slight.

[One kalpa] Here it refers to one great kalpa. A great kalpa contains four intermediate kalpas: formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness. At the end of the kalpa of destruction, fire, water, and wind calamities must arise.

[When the great kalpa burns, these four evil persons and the six hundred and four trillion people, from this Avīci great hell, are transferred to a great hell elsewhere. Why? Śāriputra, their heavy offenses are complete and their retribution is not slight; in another place they experience great suffering for countless hundreds of thousands of millions of nayuta years. When the world is formed again, these four offenders and the six hundred and four trillion people, and the others whose offenses are not yet finished, at death in that place, are born again into the great hell of this world.]

If the kalpa-fire at the end of the kalpa burns, these four evil bhikṣus and those six hundred and four trillion people, from the Avīci great hell here, are transferred to the great hell in another place. Why? Śāriputra, their heavy offenses are complete and their retribution is not slight; in the great hell elsewhere they experience great suffering for countless hundreds of thousands of millions of nayuta years. When this world is formed again, these four evil bhikṣus and those six hundred and four trillion people, together with the others whose offenses are not yet finished, at the time of their death in that place, are born again into the great hell of this world.

[Śāriputra, these four offenders and the six hundred and four trillion sentient beings, having long since been freed from the suffering of hell and born among humans, were born blind for five hundred generations. Then they encountered the Buddha of All Light — the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Fully Awakened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone One, knower of the world, the supreme being, the tamer of men, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Śāriputra, the disciples of the Buddha of All Light who heard his voice numbered one hundred million nayuta. At that time, people’s bodies were three hundred ninety-six cubits tall, and the Buddha’s body was twice that, his constant light brightly shining roundly over a hundred thousand billion yojanas.]

Śāriputra, these four evil bhikṣus and those six hundred and four trillion sentient beings, after a very long time, though freed from the suffering of hell and born among humans, were born blind for five hundred generations. Then they encountered the Buddha of All Light — the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Fully Awakened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone One, knower of the world, the supreme being, the tamer of men, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Śāriputra, the disciples of the Buddha of All Light who heard his voice numbered one hundred million nayuta. At that time, people’s bodies were three hundred ninety-six cubits tall, and the Buddha’s body was twice that, his constant light roundly shining over a hundred thousand billion yojanas.
[Cubit (zhou)] Measured by the length of the forearm. According to the Karmavācanā Commentary, one middle person’s cubit is about one foot eight inches by the Zhou dynasty measure.

[Śāriputra, these people left home in the Dharma of the Buddha of All Light and, for a hundred thousand trillion years, diligently practiced with vigor, as if saving their burning heads, yet could not obtain compliance-endurance, much less the fruit of the path! Why? Śāriputra, having created the karma of destroying anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the law of dependent conditions was such that it should be so. After their death, they were born again into the Avīci great hell, because of the karma of their earlier establishing the very heavy unwholesome causes. Śāriputra, these persons thus turned and turned, even to my present time. In between, they encountered ninety-nine hundred million Buddhas, and at the place of the Buddhas could not obtain compliance-endurance. Why? The Buddha spoke the deep sutra, but these persons did not believe it, destroyed it and went against it, slandered the wise and saintly observers of the precepts, revealed their faults, and created the karma of destroying the Dharma — the law of dependent conditions was such that it should be so.]

Śāriputra, these persons left home in the Dharma of the Buddha of All Light and, for a hundred thousand trillion years, diligently and vigorously practiced, exerting themselves as if saving their burning heads, yet could not obtain compliance-endurance, much less the fruit of the path! Why? Śāriputra, because they created the extremely heavy offense of destroying anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and in accordance with the law of dependent conditions the retribution should be so. After death they were born again into the Avīci great hell, because of the karma of their earlier establishing these very heavy unwholesome causes. Śāriputra, these persons thus turned and turned, and to this day are still suffering in the Avīci great hell. In this long interval of eons, they encountered ninety-nine hundred million Buddhas, yet at the place of the Buddhas could not obtain compliance-endurance. Why? Because the Buddha spoke the deep sutra and they did not believe it, but destroyed it and went against it, slandered the wise and saintly observers of the precepts, revealed their faults, and created the karma of destroying the Dharma — the law of dependent conditions was such that it should be so.

[Destroying the Dharma] Using wrong views to refute the Tathāgata’s true Dharma. The Lotus Sutra says: “If one hears these words, or does not believe and accept them, one creates the karma of the offense of destroying the Dharma.”

[Śāriputra, just look at them: slandering the saints, not believing the saints’ words, undergoing this immeasurable and boundless suffering, unable to gain liberation. Śāriputra, there are sentient beings who create the karma of destroying the Dharma, going against it and not believing; their number is immeasurable. At the place of ninety-nine hundred million Buddhas, through an asamkhyeya kalpa, not a single one entered nirvāṇa.]

Śāriputra, look at them: slandering the saints, not believing the saints’ words, suffering such immeasurable and boundless suffering, unable to gain liberation. Śāriputra, those sentient beings who create the karma of destroying the Dharma, going against it and not believing, are immeasurable in number. At the place of ninety-nine hundred million Buddhas, through an asamkhyeya kalpa, not a single one entered nirvāṇa.
[Asamkhyeya] That is, asamkhyeya; in Chinese it is translated “innumerable,” meaning so many that no number can count them.

[Śāriputra, who is able to destroy the Buddha’s teaching, not believing and going against it? Only ignorant worldlings, and the evil bhikṣus of overweening pride, and the bhikṣus who teach the Dharma impurely. Why? Śāriputra, these three kinds of persons are not called practitioners, not called attainers. Because they do not believe the Tathāgata’s Dharma, they slander it and go against it.]

Śāriputra, who is able to destroy the Buddha’s teaching, not believing and going against the Buddha’s words? There are three kinds: the ignorant worldling, the bhikṣu of overweening pride, and the bhikṣu who teaches the Dharma impurely. What is the reason? Śāriputra, these three kinds of persons are not called practitioners, not called attainers of the fruit. Because they do not believe the Buddha’s Dharma, they slander it and go against it.

[Śāriputra, if you ask who was the bhikṣu Ku’an who taught the Dharma impurely? He is the foolish man Devadatta of today. If you ask who was the bhikṣu of all existence who taught the Dharma impurely? He is the bhikṣu Kokālika of today. Śāriputra, if you ask who was the bhikṣu Jiangqu who taught the Dharma impurely? He is the bhikṣu Kāla of today. If you ask who was the bhikṣu Bannantu who taught the Dharma impurely? He is the naked ascetic Parimoda of today.]

Śāriputra, if you ask who was the bhikṣu Ku’an who taught the Dharma impurely? He is the foolish man Devadatta of today. If you ask who was the bhikṣu of all existence (the bhikṣu Saheduo) who taught the Dharma impurely? He is the bhikṣu Kokālika of today. Śāriputra, if you ask who was the bhikṣu Jiangqu who taught the Dharma impurely? He is the bhikṣu Kāla of today. If you ask who was the bhikṣu Bannantu who taught the Dharma impurely? He is the naked ascetic Parimoda of today.

[Devadatta] That is, Devadatta, the evil bhikṣu who, during the Buddha’s lifetime, committed the five heinous offenses and split the Order. [The five heinous offenses] Five kinds of crimes that are supremely against all reason: killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an arhat, drawing blood from a Buddha’s body, and causing a schism in the harmonious Order. Because these five are acts of extreme evil, the commission of any one of them brings one to the interminable hell; therefore they are also called the “interminable karma.”

[Śāriputra, ask yourself who at that time purely and truly spoke of the Buddhas’ bodhi, benefiting immeasurable sentient beings? It was the purity spoken by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra. Those who studied with him encountered five thousand Buddhas, and sixty-eight hundred million nayuta persons have already passed into extinction.]

Śāriputra, if you ask who at that time purely and truly spoke of the Buddhas’ bodhi and benefited immeasurable sentient beings, it is Pūrṇa of today. Those who studied and practiced with him encountered five thousand Buddhas, and sixty-eight hundred million nayuta persons have already passed into extinction.
[Pūrṇa] His full name is Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra. He was one of the ten great disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha, renowned as “foremost in preaching the Dharma.”

[Śāriputra, if a person speaks truthfully, who is the supreme Dharma-teacher, the one who decisively clarifies the Dharma and teaches it purely? It should be said that Pūrṇa is. Śāriputra, Pūrṇa, with settled mind, decisively clarified, spoke without difficulty, without there being any doubt that gave rise to debate.]

Śāriputra, if a person speaks truthfully, who is the supreme Dharma-teacher, the one who decisively clarifies the true meaning of all dharmas and teaches it purely? It is Pūrṇa. Śāriputra, because Pūrṇa’s settled mind was pure, and he decisively clarified the real nature of all dharmas, his speech was unobstructed and penetrating, so that the audience had no obscurity or doubt and no occasion for idle debate.

[Śāriputra, if a person speaks truly, who is the teacher of all dharmas of dependent causation? It should be said that Pūrṇa is. Śāriputra, in every life in which Pūrṇa was born, he constantly did the work of the Buddha for sentient beings; in the Dharma of ninety billion Buddhas, he constantly was a teacher and taught the Dharma purely. In every case, at the place of the Buddhas, to the end of his life, he always cultivated pure conduct and taught the Dharma purely.]

Śāriputra, if a person speaks truly, who is the teacher who expounds all the dharmas of dependent causation? It is Pūrṇa. Śāriputra, in life after life, Pūrṇa constantly did the work of the Buddha for sentient beings; in the Dharma of ninety billion Buddhas, he constantly was a teacher and taught the Dharma purely. In every case, at the place of the Buddhas, to the end of his life, he always cultivated pure conduct and taught the Dharma purely.
[Buddha-work (foshi)] Using the Buddha’s Dharma to teach and transform sentient beings. The Vimalakīrti Sutra

Bodhisattva chapter says: “The dignified deportment and all the actions of the Buddhas — nothing is not Buddha-work.” Kumārajīva commented: “Buddha-work means to transform sentient beings.” Later, monks and nuns performing confession rites were called doing Buddha-work. [Confession repentance (baichan)] Monks and nuns bow to the Buddha and chant sutras for the faithful to confess their offenses, or to liberate the departed. After Empress Chi of Emperor Wu of Liang died, he collected phrases from Buddhist scriptures into the ten-fascicle Liang Emperor’s Repentance Manual and had monks recite and pray. It is said this was the beginning of confession repentance. For an individual, bowing to the Buddha to seek repentance is also called baichan. [To the end of life] To the end of one’s life and body.

[Śāriputra, Pūrṇa also was a teacher in the Dharma of the six Buddhas, and in my Dharma was a great teacher, attaining arhatship and gaining liberation of mind. If a person speaks truly, who in life after life made offerings to the Buddhas and planted good roots? It should be said that Pūrṇa is. Śāriputra, in the Dharma of ninety billion Buddhas, Pūrṇa diligently sought learning and decisively debated, possessing deep wisdom; therefore the Tathāgata, among all the teachers, declared him foremost.]

Śāriputra, Pūrṇa also was a teacher in the Dharma of the six Buddhas, and in my Dharma was a great teacher, attaining the fruit of arhat and gaining liberation of mind. If a person speaks truly, who in life after life made offerings to the Buddhas and planted good roots? It is Pūrṇa. Śāriputra, in the Dharma of ninety billion Buddhas, Pūrṇa diligently sought learning, and with the principle of the real nature of all dharmas analyzed and decided all debates; possessing deep wisdom, therefore the Tathāgata declared him foremost among all the teachers.
[The six Buddhas] The six Buddhas before Śākyamuni Buddha: Vipaśyin Buddha, Śikhin Buddha, Viśvabhū Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, and Kāśyapa Buddha.

[Śāriputra, if I praised the merits of Pūrṇa for a day and a night without ceasing, even going beyond a day and a night I would still not be done. Why? Pūrṇa’s gift of the Dharma has no worldly causes, and he does not covet offerings. The teacher Pūrṇa obtained the four unobstructed knowledges; except for the Tathāgata, among all things in the world there is no one who can surpass him in words and meaning.]

Śāriputra, if I spent a day and a night praising the merits of Pūrṇa, I could not finish; spending another day and a night, still I could not finish. Why? Because Pūrṇa’s gift of the Dharma has no worldly causes and he does not covet fame and offerings. The teacher Pūrṇa obtained the four unobstructed knowledges; except for the Tathāgata, among all things in the world there is no one who can surpass him in words and meaning.
[The four unobstructed knowledges] The unobstructed knowledge of dharmas, of meanings, of eloquence, and of joyful speech.

[Śāriputra, I now tell you: if a person wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and preaches the Dharma for others, they obtain immeasurable and boundless merit, and are also able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings. Śāriputra, if a person destroys it, goes against it, and does not believe this Dharma, then they create immeasurable causes of heavy offense. Why? Śāriputra, evil has evil retribution and good has good retribution. For this reason I now entrust this sutra to you, and it should be widely explained and distinguished for the four assemblies.]

Śāriputra, I now tell you: if a person wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and preaches the Dharma for others, they obtain immeasurable and boundless merit, and are also able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings. Śāriputra, if a person destroys it, goes against it, and does not believe this Dharma, they create immeasurable causes of heavy offense. Why? Śāriputra, evil has evil retribution and good has good retribution. For this reason I now entrust this sutra to you; it should be carefully explained and widely propagated for the four assemblies.
[Entrust (zhulei)] Entrusting a matter to another and asking them to take the labor upon themselves. [The four assemblies] Monks, nuns, laymen (upāsaka), and laywomen (upāsikā).

[Śāriputra, if one hears this sutra and believes with a joyful heart, one immediately obtains immeasurable and boundless merit. If one hears it without believing, the mind not rejoicing, one immediately obtains immeasurable and boundless heavy offense. Śāriputra, you should know that such a person is called a precept-breaking bhikṣu, one of overweening pride, one who teaches the Dharma impurely. Śāriputra, if a person goes against this teaching, in every life in which they are born they are always blind, without eyes.]

Śāriputra, if a person hears this sutra (the Sutra on the Buddha’s Treasury) and believes with a joyful heart, they immediately obtain immeasurable and boundless merit. If one hears it without believing, the mind not rejoicing, one immediately obtains immeasurable and boundless heavy offense. Śāriputra, you should know that such a person is called a precept-breaking bhikṣu, one of overweening pride, one who teaches the Dharma impurely. Śāriputra, if a person goes against this sutra and does not believe it, they obtain evil retribution, and in life after life are always blind, without eyes.

[Śāriputra, I now clearly tell you. What I now speak is not like a potter cherishing unfired clay vessels. I now clearly, for the four assemblies, speak the foremost meaning, the ultimately-empty Dharma. Those who are firm remain; those who are not firm break. Why? Śāriputra, the Buddha, having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, does not preach the Dharma for evil persons of wrong views, nor for those with the view of self, view of person, view of sentient being, or view of life. Why? All these attachments are called wrong views. Śāriputra, one with such a view of self and view of person cannot obtain compliance-endurance, much less the fruit of the path! Śāriputra, if one with a view of self, view of person, view of sentient being, view of life, annihilationist view, or eternalist view could obtain compliance-endurance and the fruit of the path — there is no such possibility!]

Śāriputra, I now clearly tell you. What I now speak is not like a potter cherishing unfired clay vessels. I now clearly, for the four assemblies, speak the foremost meaning, the ultimately-empty Dharma. Those who are firm remain; those who are not firm break. Why? Śāriputra, the Buddha, having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, does not preach the Dharma for evil persons of wrong views, nor for those with the view of self, view of person, view of sentient being, or view of life. Why? Because all these attachments are called wrong views. Śāriputra, one with such a view of self, view of person, view of sentient being, and view of life cannot obtain compliance-endurance, much less the fruit of the path! Śāriputra, if one with a view of self, view of person, view of sentient being, view of life, annihilationist view, or eternalist view could obtain compliance-endurance and the fruit of the path, there is no such possibility!
[There is no such possibility] There is not the slightest correctness in it. This means: it is entirely wrong and impossible.

[Therefore, Śāriputra, if a person accomplishes such views, in my Dharma I do not allow them to receive offerings. They are not practitioners, nor attainers; rather, in my Dharma they merely seek to keep themselves alive. Śāriputra, I say that an outsider who wishes to enter the Buddha’s Dharma should be tested for four months. Why? Outsiders mostly have the view of self, view of person, view of sentient being, view of life, annihilationist view, and eternalist view.]

For this reason, Śāriputra, if a person accomplishes such views (the view of self, view of person, view of sentient being, view of life, annihilationist view, and eternalist view), in my Dharma I do not allow them to receive offerings. They are not practitioners, nor attainers of the path, but in the Buddha’s Dharma merely seek worldly gain and to keep themselves alive. Śāriputra, I say that an outsider who wishes to enter the Buddha’s gate should first be examined for four months, and then a decision made as to whether to allow them to leave home and receive the precepts. Why? Because outsiders mostly have the view of self, view of person, view of sentient being, view of life, annihilationist view, and eternalist view.

[Śāriputra, my disciples have no view of self, view of person, view of sentient being, view of life, annihilationist view, or eternalist view. My disciples only speak of the endurance of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-attainment, and speak of consciousness as dwelling nowhere. Śāriputra, if a person accomplishes such endurance, I allow this person to leave home and receive the precepts, and to receive offerings of robes, food, bedding, and medicine. If a person does not have such endurance, they should first be tested and first taught to abide in the selflessness of all dharmas.]

Śāriputra, my disciples have no view of self, view of person, view of sentient being, view of life, annihilationist view, or eternalist view. My disciples only speak of the endurance of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-attainment, and speak of consciousness as dwelling nowhere. Śāriputra, if a person accomplishes such endurance of non-attainment, I allow this person to leave home and receive the precepts, and to receive offerings of robes, food, bedding, and medicine. If this person does not have such endurance, they should first be tested, and first be taught to abide in the selflessness of all dharmas.

[The endurance of non-attainment] The Heart Sutra says: “Because there is nothing to attain, the bodhisattva, relying on the perfection of wisdom, has no hindrance in mind; because there is no hindrance, there is no fear, and far from all inverted dreams, they reach ultimate nirvāṇa.” [The selflessness of all dharmas] That is, all dharmas have no self-nature; that is, all dharmas have no real substance, being illusions.

[Śāriputra, if one does not rejoice in this endurance, and hearing of the foremost meaning of emptiness is startled, doubts, and derides, while hearing of the view of self one’s mind rejoices; you should know that such a person is driven by Māra, one who is a former outsider.]

Śāriputra, if a person does not rejoice in this endurance (abiding in the selflessness of all dharmas), and hearing of the foremost meaning of emptiness becomes startled, doubts, and derides, while hearing of the view of self the mind rejoices, you should know that such a person is driven by Māra, and one who comes to destroy the Buddha’s Dharma, like the outsider spoken of earlier.

[Śāriputra, the wise should not be grieved over this, but should give rise to compassion toward such a person. Why? Śāriputra, if a person accomplishes such evils, the evil retribution they obtain is inexpressible. Toward this person one should give rise to a mind of benefit, teaching the selflessness of all dharmas, the emptiness and stillness of all dharmas, the non-action of all dharmas, and that there is no recipient. If this person loves the Buddha’s Dharma and, hearing these things, the mind rejoices, then the other bhikṣus of the practice of emptiness, the non-attainers, should all show, teach, benefit, and gladden them, comforting their minds and speaking to them of the Dharma of the non-existence of all things, emptiness.]

Śāriputra, the wise, toward those who do not believe the true Dharma and give rise to wrong views, should not be grieved, but should give rise to a mind of compassion toward such a person. Why? Śāriputra, if a person accomplishes such evil karma, the evil retribution they obtain is inexpressible. Toward this person one should give rise to a mind of benefit, teaching the selflessness of all dharmas, the emptiness and stillness of all dharmas, the non-action of all dharmas, and that there is no recipient. If this person, hearing such Dharma, gives rise to joy of mind, then the other bhikṣus of the practice of emptiness, the non-attainers, should all show, teach, benefit, and gladden them, comforting their minds and speaking to them of the Dharma of the non-existence of all things, emptiness.

[Show, teach, benefit, and gladden] That is: show, teach, benefit, and gladden. These are the four stages of the Buddha’s teaching and transforming: first, show, i.e., reveal the meaning; second, teach, i.e., instruct in the practice; third, benefit, i.e., obtain the meaning and profit; fourth, gladden, i.e., praise their correct practice and make the mind rejoice. The Lotus Sutra

Parable of the Phantom City chapter says: “Show, teach, benefit, and gladden, causing them to arouse the mind for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” [Meaning and benefit] Meaning and benefit correspond; meaning must have benefit, hence it is called meaning-and-benefit. The Buddhabhūmi-sūtra Commentary says: “Meaning and benefit — present benefit is called meaning, future benefit is called benefit.” The Mahāvairocana-ābhisaṃbodhi Commentary says: “In each and every mantra there is the ability to accomplish all meaning and benefit.”

[If one hears it and is startled and afraid, one should, in the assembly, tell his upādhyāya and ācārya. As the sutra says of one who practices the practice of emptiness, and who is also able to know the distinct characteristics of all dharmas, I am his teacher; I am not the teacher of those with the view of self, view of person, inverted wrong views, or of those who, greedily clinging to the precepts, make them a teacher.]

If this person, hearing “the non-existence of all things, emptiness,” is startled and afraid, one should give rise to compassion and, in the midst of the great assembly, tell his upādhyāya and ācārya, so as to instruct and transform him. If he is like the practitioner of the emptiness practice spoken of in the sutra, and is also able to know the distinct characteristics of all dharmas, then I (the World-Honored One) am his teacher, and am not the teacher of those with the view of self, view of person, inverted wrong views, or of those who, not well versed in what is allowed and prohibited, and in pure observance of the precepts, instead greedily cling to the precepts.

[Upādhyāya (heshang)] Also written as “heshang”; it means “my teacher,” a respectful term the monks use for their personal instructor. [Ācārya (āshēlí)] In Chinese it is translated “guide of the norms”; that is, the bhikṣu who corrects the conduct of his disciples. [Distinct characteristics] The characteristics by which each thing differs from others. That which follows conditions and is without self-nature is the general characteristic of all dharmas; that which is without self-nature yet follows conditions is the distinct characteristic of all dharmas.

[The Tathāgata permits those with right views to participate in the upoṣatha, but does not permit those who break the precepts or who, holding wrong views, break the deportment, to participate in the upoṣatha. If elders and their disciples, hearing the Dharma of emptiness, stillness, and non-existence, do not believe and rejoice, their minds intent on outsiders, the Buddha does not allow them to participate in the upoṣatha with outsiders. If such persons do not abandon this view, they should not be allowed to take part in the affairs of the Saṅgha, nor should their requests be accepted. If, having done this, they still do not abandon it, you should know that such persons are not on the path, but are forever abandoned. One should speak to their upādhyāya and ācārya, and they should not be kept any longer. Śāriputra, if the Saṅgha is thus, then it makes offerings to me, and also well refutes the wrong views of outsiders; this is called the pure preaching of the precepts at the upoṣatha.]

The Tathāgata permits those with right views to participate in the upoṣatha, but does not permit those who break the precepts or, holding wrong views, break the deportment, to participate in the upoṣatha. If elders and their disciples, hearing the Dharma of emptiness, stillness, and non-existence, do not believe and rejoice, their minds intent on outsiders, the Buddha does not allow them to participate in the upoṣatha. If these persons still do not abandon their wrong views, they should not be allowed to participate in the affairs of the Saṅgha, nor should their requests be accepted. If, after such measures, they still do not abandon the views, you should know that they are not on the right path, but are forever abandoned from the path of enlightenment. One should tell their upādhyāya and ācārya, and drive them out of the Saṅgha. Śāriputra, if the Saṅgha can thus possess right views, it makes offerings to the Tathāgata, and also well refutes the wrong views of outsiders; this is called the pure preaching of the precepts at the upoṣatha.

[Upoṣatha (busala)] In Chinese it is translated “pure abiding” or “growth.” Every half-month (the fifteenth day and the twenty-ninth or thirtieth day), the monks gather and preach the precept-sutra, causing the bhikṣus to abide in the pure precepts and to be able to grow in good dharmas. [They should not be kept any longer] Drive them out of the Saṅgha. Once, at an upoṣatha, the Buddha sat in silence. Through the first and middle watches of the night, the Buddha was always silent. Maudgalyāyana, observing with his supernormal powers, saw a precept-breaker sitting not far from the Buddha, and drove him out. [Deportment] The dignified virtue and rules that should accompany walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. The Contemplation of Amitāyus Sutra says: “Perfect in all the precepts, not violating the deportment.”

[Śāriputra, I now clearly tell you: if a person accepts this view of self, view of person, view of sentient being, and view of existence and non-existence, this person is not called making offerings to me, not called following me in leaving home and receiving the precepts; this is called following the six teachers in leaving home, taking the six teachers as his teachers.]

Sariputra, I now tell you plainly: if a person accepts the view of self, the view of persons, the view of sentient beings, the view of existence or non-existence, such a person cannot be said to make offerings to the Buddha, cannot be said to have left home and received the precepts following the Buddha; rather, he has left home following the six non-Buddhist teachers and taken them as his teachers.
Sariputra, if a person cannot attain forbearance in this pure and true Dharma and yet receives offerings, what that person receives is wrongfully received.
Sariputra, if a person cannot abide in the Dharma of pure true characteristics and yet receives offerings, the offerings that person receives are wrongly received.

Sariputra, though such a person has left home within my Dharma and upheld pure precepts, yet toward the supreme-meaning emptiness, the Dharma of non-attainment, his mind does not believe or understand, and he is alarmed, frightened, doubtful, and regretful. Know that such a person prizes only precepts, much learning, and dhyana. Sariputra, such a person cannot be said to make offerings to me, to honor me, or to respect me. Why? Sariputra, from beginnings time there has been no sentient being who has not attained the four dhyanas. If one merely knows the four dhyanas and calls that the benefit of a renunciant, how can such a person be said to make offerings to me?

Sariputra, though such a person has left home within my Dharma and upholds pure precepts, yet toward the supreme-meaning emptiness, the Dharma of non-attainment, his mind neither believes nor understands, and he is alarmed, frightened, doubtful, and regretful. Know that this person prizes only precepts, much learning, and dhyana. Sariputra, this person cannot be said to make offerings to me, to honor me, or to respect me. Why? Sariputra, from beginnings time there has been no sentient being who has not attained the four dhyanas. Those who think only that by attaining the four dhyanas they have gained the benefit of a renunciant have not entered the way of the Buddha; how can they be said to make offerings to me?

[Yet prizing only precepts, much learning, and dhyana] If one can only uphold precepts, be learned, and practice dhyana, one can only be reborn among humans and devas; one has not yet left the three realms and cannot put an end to birth and death. [The four dhyanas] The first, second, third, and fourth dhyanas are concentration practices also cultivated by ordinary people and non-Buddhist teachers; by cultivating them one may be reborn in the various heavens of the form realm: the heaven of the first dhyana, the heaven of the second dhyana, the heaven of the third dhyana, and the heaven of the fourth dhyana.

Therefore, Sariputra, I now tell you plainly: people of future times will, within my Dharma, cling and grasp in various ways, hold various wrong views, and destroy my Dharma. Sariputra, if a person prizes only precepts, much learning, and dhyana, know that this person cannot purely practice the various dharmas of a renunciant, and I do not call such a person a renunciant, a brahmin. Sariputra, if a person sees that all dharmas are without self and truly knows the absence of self; that all dharmas are originally without anything existing, empty, and truly knows that originally nothing exists and all is empty — such a person does not take precepts as supreme, much learning as supreme, or dhyana as supreme. Why? Sariputra, the true characteristics of all dharmas are unborn and unarisen; within them there is no dharma that can be supreme. Sariputra, in the truth of these dharmas there is no one who observes precepts and no one who breaks precepts — how much less can one cling to them and regard them as supreme?

Therefore, Sariputra, I now tell you plainly: people of future times, within the Buddha Dharma, will give rise to various clingings and graspings, various wrong views, and destroy the Buddha Dharma. Sariputra, if a person prizes only precepts, much learning, and dhyana, know that this person cannot purely practice the various dharmas of a renunciant; I do not call such a person a pure practitioner among renunciants. Sariputra, if a person sees that all dharmas are without self and truly knows the absence of self, and that all dharmas are originally without anything existing and empty and truly knows this, such a person will not take precepts as supreme, much learning as supreme, or dhyana as supreme. Why? Sariputra, the true characteristics of all dharmas are unborn and unarisen; within them no dharma can be supreme. Sariputra, in the truth of these dharmas there is no one who observes precepts and no one who breaks precepts; how much less can one cling to precepts, much learning, and dhyana as really existing and regard them as supreme?
[Brahmin] It means “pure conduct” and is also one of the four castes of India. Here it carries the meaning of “pure conduct.”

Sariputra, this is called the Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas. It means that all dharmas are without characteristics, their own nature is empty, with no self and no person. If one attains this forbearance, one is called a practitioner, one is called an attainer. Such a person is called one who has left home through faith and is worthy of receiving offerings and of pure uposatha; such a person is a deva among humans.

Sariputra, all dharmas are originally without anything existing and empty; this is called the supreme right and perfect enlightenment (Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi) of all Buddhas. This means that all dharmas are without characteristics, their own nature is empty, with no self and no person. If a person can abide in this principle, he is called a practitioner, he is called an attainer. Such a person is called one who has left home through right faith, is worthy of receiving offerings, should take part in the pure uposatha, and is a deva among humans.

Sariputra, the Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas is a single meaning, namely, separation. What is separation? Separation from all desires and all views. Desire is ignorance, and view is recollection. Why? All dharmas have recollection as their root. All thoughts and imaginings are views, and views are wrong. Sariputra, even a view arisen within wholesome dharmas I call a wrong view. Why? Sariputra, in separation from desire and in still extinction there is no dharma and no non-dharma, no good and no evil — all these things are empty. Being far from all bonds and all recollection is therefore called separation. Sariputra, within the supreme Way all desires are forever stilled. What are these desires? They are the evil and unwholesome thoughts: the thought of self, of mine, of creating characteristics, of phenomenal characteristics. This is called the forever-stilling of all desires within the Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

Sariputra, the Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas is a single meaning, namely, separation. Separation from what? Separation from all desires and all views. Desire is ignorance, and view is recollection. Why? Because all dharmas have recollection as their root. All thoughts and imaginings are views, and views are wrong. Sariputra, even if a view arises within wholesome dharmas, I call it a wrong view. Why? Sariputra, in separation from desire and in still extinction there is no dharma and no non-dharma, no good and no evil; all these things are entirely without anything existing. Being far from all desires and all recollection, that is separation. Sariputra, within the supreme Way all desires are forever stilled. What are these desires? They are the evil and unwholesome recollections, such as the view of self, the view of what is mine, and the characteristics of creation and of phenomena, and so on. All being separated, this is called the forever-stilling of all desires within the Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

[All bonds] All desires. “Bond” means what binds and ties; here it refers to “desire.” Desire is the root of afflictions, binding the cultivator of the Way so that he cannot gain liberation and sinks in birth and death.

blocks.text: 9. The Chapter on Comprehending the Precepts

inline.s: In this chapter the Blessed One teaches: there are three kinds of people who do not delight in hearing this scripture (the Buddha’s Treasury Sutra): first, monks who break the precepts; second, those of arrogant conceit; third, those who teach impurely and cling to a self. He then explains that a portion of the Tathagata’s white hair-mark light can suffice to support monks who cultivate the Way according to the Dharma; such monks need not worry about the four necessities (clothing, food, bedding, and medicine) but should single-mindedly practice the Way.

The Buddha told Sariputra: There are three kinds of people who, upon hearing this scripture, do not delight in it. What are the three? First, monks who break the precepts; second, those of arrogant conceit; third, those who teach impurely and cling to a self. These people are far from this profound scripture that accords with true characteristics, and are fully filled by the faction of the born-blind.

The Buddha told Sariputra: There are three kinds of people who, upon hearing this scripture, do not delight in it. Which three? First, monks who break the precepts; second, those of arrogant conceit; third, those who teach impurely and cling to a self. These people are far from this profound scripture that accords with the true characteristics of all dharmas; they are wholly the faction formed by the ignorant born-blind.
[Faction] A clique. [Clique] A group or sect that bands together for private gain.

Therefore, Sariputra, I entrust this scripture to you again with solemn charge. Why? Because after the Tathagata’s extinction this scripture can cause pure, precept-observing monks to give rise to joy in their hearts. Such a profound scripture is ever upheld by those of pure precepts and ever kept far from by those who break the precepts. Why? Because when a foolish person hears true and right words, he regards them as a hardship.

For this reason, Sariputra, I again entrust this scripture to you with solemn charge. Why? Because after the Tathagata’s extinction this scripture can cause pure, precept-observing monks to give rise to joy in their hearts. Such a profound scripture is ever upheld by those of pure precepts and ever kept far from by those who break the precepts. Why do those who break the precepts keep far from it? Because a foolish person who breaks the precepts, upon hearing true and right words, regards them as a hardship.

Sariputra, the characteristics produced by monks who break the precepts, the Tathagata has already fully set forth here. Sariputra, a monk who breaks the precepts naturally does not delight in observing the precepts and proper conduct; a foolish person does not delight in wisdom; a miserly person does not wish to hear of giving; one of arrogant conceit does not wish to hear this Dharma free of arrogance. If they hear it they are alarmed and fearful as if falling into a deep pit. Those fond of worldly gain cling to fine flavors, and upon hearing the reproof of craving food, their minds become distressed and troubled.

Sariputra, the various characteristics of sin of monks who break the precepts I have already set forth in detail here (in the third chapter, on recollecting the Dharma, the fourth chapter, on recollecting the Sangha, and the fifth chapter, on pure precepts, the Blessed One explained in detail the various characteristics of sin of monks who break the precepts, culminating in the ten arrows of distress and the certainty of falling into evil realms). Sariputra, a monk who breaks the precepts naturally does not delight in observing the precepts and proper conduct; a foolish person naturally does not delight in wisdom; a miserly and greedy person naturally does not wish to hear of giving; one of arrogant conceit naturally does not wish to hear this Dharma free of arrogance. If they hear this scripture they are alarmed and fearful as if falling into a deep pit, like those fond of worldly pleasure who cling to fine flavors and, upon hearing the reproof of craving food, become distressed and troubled in mind.

[Vinaya and deportment] Vinaya is the precepts, deportment is the rules of conduct. The precepts laid down by the Buddha guard people against wrongdoing and stop evil; they are the rules of conduct by which a disciple of the Buddha stands and deals with the world. [He] Same as “he,” to reproach. [Zi
zǐ
] to criticize.

Those who delight in reading non-Buddhist scriptures give rise within them to thoughts of solid reality; those who cling to words delight in speaking of scattered things; those who delight in adorning their speech with clever and beautiful phrases have no pure mind toward the Buddha’s supreme meaning, and moreover neither revere nor believe in this Dharma. Sariputra, it is like a eunuch who has no use as a man: among men he conceives the thought of being a eunuch and thinks, ‘These people are all just like me.’ So too those who are fond of clinging to non-Buddhist scriptures ever delight in adorning their words with clever, beautiful phrases, and have no reverent mind toward the Buddha’s supreme meaning.

Those who delight in reading non-Buddhist scriptures (monks fallen into non-Buddhist doctrines) give rise within these non-Buddhist scriptures to thoughts of solid reality. They cling to words, delight in fine-sounding talk, delight in adorning their phrasing, and delight in wielding the brush. Toward the Buddha’s supreme meaning they have no settled pure mind, and toward this holy Dharma they neither revere nor believe. Sariputra, it is like a eunuch who has no use as a man: among men he thinks others are also eunuchs, thinking, ‘These people are all just like me.’ So too those fond of non-Buddhist scriptures ever delight in adorning clever, beautiful phrases and have no reverent mind toward the Buddha’s supreme meaning.

Sariputra, if among them someone speaks a pure scripture, they are likewise not reverent toward that person and slight the pure, precept-observing monks. Why? Sariputra, non-Buddhist scriptures contain no true words, and by their nature they should breed arrogance, haughtiness, and self-importance. Why? These matters are not for the sake of revulsion, not for still extinction, not for attaining the Way, not for nirvana. Because such people have destroyed the wholesome roots of faith and so forth, they do not believe that there is merit anywhere, like a eunuch who among all men thinks each is like himself.

Sariputra, if among them someone speaks a pure scripture, they (monks fallen into non-Buddhist doctrines) are likewise not reverent toward that person and slight the pure, precept-observing monks. Why? Sariputra, non-Buddhist scriptures contain no true words, and those who have fallen into non-Buddhist doctrines naturally become arrogant, haughty, and self-important. Why? Because they do not seek revulsion from birth and death, do not seek still extinction, do not seek the Way, do not seek nirvana — they only seek to keep themselves alive, only seek fame and profit. Because these people have destroyed their own five wholesome roots of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, they do not believe that there is merit anywhere, nor do they believe that there exist people of merit, like a eunuch who among all men thinks everyone else is a eunuch like himself.

Sariputra, it is like one blind from birth who does not see the various colors — what are called black and white; he does not see black and white, does not see beautiful and ugly colors, does not see blue, yellow, red, white, red, purple, and azure tones, does not see the colors of long and short, coarse and fine, shallow and deep, does not see the sun, moon, and stars, and does not see those who see the sun, moon, and stars. Such a blind person then thinks: there is no black and white, no one who sees black and white; there are no beautiful and ugly colors, no blue, yellow, purple, azure tones, no long and short, coarse and fine, shallow and deep, no colors of the sun, moon, and stars, and no one who sees them; all other people are the same. The blind person’s mind is inverted, and everywhere he deems it dark.

Sariputra, they (monks who break the precepts, those of arrogant conceit, and monks fallen into non-Buddhist doctrines) are like one blind from birth who cannot see the various colors, shapes, and objects; he cannot see black and white, cannot see beautiful and ugly colors, cannot see the colors of blue, yellow, red, white, red, purple, and azure, cannot see the colors of long and short, coarse and fine, shallow and deep, cannot see the sun, moon, and stars. Such a blind person then thinks: there is no black and white, and no one who sees black and white; there are no beautiful and ugly colors, no blue, yellow, red, white, red, purple, and azure, no long and short, coarse and fine, shallow and deep, no sun, moon, and stars, and no one who sees the beautiful and ugly colors, the blue, yellow, red, white, red, purple, and azure, the long and short, coarse and fine, shallow and deep, and the sun, moon, and stars. The blind person’s mind is inverted, and everywhere he deems it darkness.

The Blessed One again uses the simile of the one blind from birth who cannot see the various colors to show that monks who break the precepts, those of arrogant conceit, and monks fallen into non-Buddhist doctrines have inverted minds, thinking that others are like them in breaking the precepts, in arrogant conceit, and in falling into non-Buddhist doctrines; everywhere they do not believe there is merit, nor do they believe there exist people of merit.

Sariputra, monks who break the precepts, those of arrogant conceit, and monks fallen into non-Buddhist doctrines are likewise. Toward the profound Buddha Dharma their minds neither believe nor delight, and they cannot penetrate it; hearing that all dharmas are empty and without anything existing, they neither believe nor delight, and cannot penetrate it. Sariputra, such people are afraid of you, enter the boundary of the wrong, and do not obtain the right Dharma. Because this right Dharma is called the true renunciant, such people do not believe in the Dharma you have obtained, like a blind man who says there is no black, white, or other color. Sariputra, such people enter the boundary of the wrong, seek non-Buddhist doctrines, delight in noisy chatter, and increase afflictions, evil nature, and evil dharmas; they cannot believe that all dharmas are empty, much less penetrate it.

Sariputra, monks who break the precepts, those of arrogant conceit, and monks fallen into non-Buddhist doctrines are likewise. Toward the profound Buddha Dharma their minds neither believe nor delight and they cannot penetrate it; hearing that all dharmas are empty and without anything existing, they neither believe nor delight and cannot penetrate it. Sariputra, these people are afraid of you (because you have deeply attained the Buddha’s right Dharma); they enter into wrong dharmas and do not obtain the right Dharma. Therefore, only one who obtains the right Dharma is called a true renunciant. These people do not believe in the right Dharma you have obtained, like a blind man who thinks there is no black, white, or other color. Sariputra, such people enter into wrong dharmas, seek non-Buddhist doctrines, delight in noisy chatter, and increase afflictions, evil nature, and evil dharmas; they cannot believe that all dharmas are empty, much less penetrate it.

Sariputra, what do you think: a jackal as a lion — could it already roar, now roar, and future roar, and do the lion’s walking — now walking, future walking, already walked? Not so, World-Honored One. Why? The jackal’s color, strength, and voice do not measure up to the lion’s; a jackal can only make a jackal’s sound. If it wishes to make sound, only a jackal’s sound comes forth, not a lion’s.

Sariputra, what do you think? A jackal wishing to make a lion’s roar — could it already roar, now roar, and future (to come) roar? A jackal wishing to do the lion’s walking — could it now walk, future walk, and already walked? Sariputra replied: It could not, World-Honored One. Why? The jackal’s color, strength, and voice all do not measure up to the lion’s; a jackal can only make a jackal’s sound. If it wishes to make sound, only a jackal’s sound comes forth, and not a lion’s.
[Jackal] In color blue-yellow like a dog, small in form with a tail large like a fox’s; it moves in packs and cries at night, its voice like a wolf’s.

The Blessed One uses the simile of the jackal wishing to make a lion’s roar to show that monks who break the precepts, those of arrogant conceit, and monks fallen into non-Buddhist doctrines vainly try to disguise their wrong doctrines and absurd theories as the Buddha Dharma to delude sentient beings; yet however much wrong doctrines and absurd theories are disguised, they remain in the end wrong doctrines and absurd theories (a jackal’s cry is still a jackal’s cry).

Thus, Sariputra, monks who break the precepts and monks of arrogant conceit take this matter as supreme, and those who teach impurely accept the doctrines of the Nirgranthas. If they cling to one matter and hold it fast without letting it go, are greedy for worldly profit, delight in reading scriptures, and cannot penetrate the true characteristics of all dharmas — if such people could believe and accept the signless Dharma, that would be impossible.

Thus, Sariputra, monks who break the precepts and monks of arrogant conceit take this matter (the jackal disguised as a lion) as supreme, and those who teach impurely accept the wrong doctrines of non-Buddhist teachers. If they cling to one matter and hold it fast without letting it go — for example, being greedy for worldly profit, delighting in reading non-Buddhist scriptures, and so on — they cannot possibly penetrate the true characteristics of all dharmas. If such people could believe and accept the signless Dharma, that would be utterly impossible.

Sariputra, if there is a monk of venerable age and virtue, a lion among monks, with deep wisdom, that person can believe in the Dharma of non-attainment, of emptiness of self-nature, the Dharma of no self and no person. Why? This person does not delight in noisy mixed talk, does not delight in reading scriptures, sleeping, and being busy with many affairs; does not manage worldly affairs for laypeople, does not serve as a messenger carrying documents, does not practice medicine, does not read medical prescriptions, does not engage in trade, and does not delight in discussing worldly speech; but only delights in speaking transcendent speech. This person can believe that all dharmas are empty, and toward all dharmas neither gives rise to nor destroys them; this person can then realize the true limit and can truly roar the lion’s roar — not a jackal’s cry.

Sariputra, if there is a monk of venerable age (referring to the many years since his ordination) and virtue, a lion among monks, with deep wisdom, that person can believe in the Dharma of non-attainment, of emptiness of self-nature, the Dharma of no self and no person. Why? This person does not delight in noisy mixed talk, does not delight in reading scriptures, sleeping, and being busy with many affairs; does not manage worldly affairs for others, does not serve as a messenger carrying documents, does not practice medicine, does not read medical prescriptions, does not engage in trade, and does not delight in discussing worldly speech; but only delights in speaking transcendent speech. This person can believe that all dharmas are empty, can believe that all dharmas neither arise nor cease, and can then realize the true characteristics of all dharmas and truly roar the lion’s roar — not a jackal’s cry.

Sariputra, if there is a monk who clings to the meaning of external scriptures, that person has abandoned the subtle Buddha Dharma. He recites and upholds non-Buddhist words and speaks them to the great assembly, but only makes the cry of a jackal. Sariputra, such an evil person is called a rotten renunciant. Why? Because those non-Buddhist doctrines are not the Buddha Dharma.

Sariputra, if there is a monk who accepts the meaning of non-Buddhist scriptures, that person has abandoned the subtle Buddha Dharma. They recite and uphold non-Buddhist words and speak them to the great assembly, making the cry of a jackal. Sariputra, such an evil person is called a rotten renunciant. Why? Because what they propagate are the wrong doctrines of non-Buddhist teachers, and not the Buddha Dharma.

Sariputra, a monk who clings to non-Buddhist dharmas should not call himself a disciple of the Buddha. Why? A son of the Shakyas who is a renunciant does not speak the words of the Nirgranthas; among the great assembly he speaks only the words of the Buddha. Sariputra, if a person clings to impure words and wishes to make a lion’s roar, he only makes a jackal’s cry. That person cannot understand the supreme meaning of the Buddha Dharma.

Sariputra, a monk who accepts non-Buddhist dharmas should not call himself a disciple of the Buddha. Why? A son of the Shakyas who is a renunciant does not speak non-Buddhist words; among the great assembly he speaks only the words of the Buddha. Sariputra, if a person accepts non-Buddhist dharmas and wishes to make a lion’s roar, it is only a jackal’s cry. That person cannot understand the supreme meaning of the Buddha Dharma.

Sariputra, I now tell you plainly: if a person is fully endowed with precepts, dhyana, and wisdom; is neither miserly nor greedy, not defiled by anger or delusion, not harboring flattery and crookedness, and has a mind of revulsion; whose words are always true, who ever delights in solitude, does not delight in sleep, delights in the practice of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, of non-arising and non-ceasing, and gives rise to a mind of separation from desire, seeking to understand the supreme meaning of the Buddha Dharma; who does not care for worldly speech, delights in transcendent speech, fully upholds all the precepts, and is far from all evil matters and evil spiritual friends — abiding in such dharmas, this person can understand the Dharma of emptiness and non-attainment. Why? Sariputra, this practice is called the practice of the great man; it is not the practice of one who delights in profit and support, not the practice of the foolish and ordinary, not the practice of a corrupted renunciant, not the practice of a dregs renunciant, not the practice of a nominal renunciant.

Sariputra, I now tell you plainly: if a person is fully endowed with precepts, dhyana, and wisdom; is neither miserly nor greedy, not defiled by anger or delusion, not harboring flattery and crookedness, and has no mind of revulsion toward the right Dharma; whose words are always true, who ever delights in solitude, does not delight in sleep, delights in the practice of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, of non-arising and non-ceasing, and gives rise to a mind of separation from desire, seeking to understand the supreme meaning of the Buddha Dharma; who does not care for worldly speech, delights in transcendent speech, fully upholds all the precepts, and is far from all evil matters and evil spiritual friends — abiding in such dharmas, this person can understand the Dharma of emptiness and non-attainment. Why? Sariputra, this practice is called the practice of a bodhisattva; it is not the practice of one who delights in profit and support, not the practice of the foolish and ordinary, not the practice of a corrupted renunciant, not the practice of a dregs renunciant, not the practice of a nominal (in name only) renunciant.
[Great man] One in a high position; here it refers to a bodhisattva.

Sariputra, the true characteristics of all dharmas, ultimately empty and still, are the very Buddha Way. Those fond of worldly wealth and profit, and greedy to speak impure dharmas, cannot reach it. Sariputra, this ground is called the ground of great wisdom; it is not the ground of those who delight in non-Buddhist teachings, nor the ground of those who speak of the view of self or the view of persons.

Sariputra, the true characteristics of all dharmas, ultimately empty and still, are the very Buddha Way. Those fond of worldly wealth and profit, and greedy to speak impure dharmas, cannot reach it. Sariputra, this ground is called the ground of great wisdom; it is not the ground of those who delight in non-Buddhist teachings, nor the ground of those who speak of the view of self and the view of persons.

[Those greedy to speak impure dharmas] Earlier, in the sixth chapter on the pure Dharma, the Blessed One said: “Those who speak impurely have five faults. What are the five? First, they claim for themselves to know the whole Buddha Dharma; second, when speaking the Buddha’s scriptures they bring up apparent contradictions among the scriptures (some do not know that the Buddha spoke the Dharma according to the two truths; with regard to ordinary beings he speaks of conditioned existence as real — the conventional truth; with regard to sages he speaks of emptiness as real — the supreme truth. Those who speak impurely only know how to grasp characteristics and do not grasp the meaning, and so say the scriptures are self-contradictory); third, in their minds they doubt and do not believe the various dharmas; fourth, by what they know they condemn the scriptures of others (recklessly criticizing the scriptures by their own ideas); fifth, for the sake of profit and support they teach the Dharma for people. Sariputra, of those who speak thus, I say such people will fall into hell and not reach nirvana.”

Sariputra, if there truly were a self and persons, then those who speak of self and persons should have true characteristics. One should ask in truth: if there is a self, what color is it — blue, yellow, red, or white? Is it within the body or outside the body? Does it pervade the body like oil in sesame? Sariputra, oil in sesame can be extracted and shown; if a self were within, one who says there is a self should point it out and show it, as one extracts oil from sesame and shows the oil. Within the supreme meaning, seeking a self, it cannot be obtained. Therefore know that if one speaks of self and persons, that person does not yet have the precepts of a renunciant, much less the ground of a renunciant.

One should ask in truth: if there is a self, what color is it — blue, yellow, red, or white? Is it within the body or outside the body? Does it pervade the whole body like oil in sesame?
