Within the supreme meaning, seeking a self, it cannot be obtained. Therefore know that if one speaks of self and persons, that person does not yet have the precepts of a renunciant, much less the ground of a renunciant.

Sariputra, know that those who cling wrongly in this way — clinging to self, clinging to sentient beings, clinging to life and lifespan — fall from the crown. Because such people cling wrongly in this way, they cannot even remove the mind greedy for profit and support, much less the subtle afflictions. Sariputra, for one who has penetrated emptiness, to be covered by greed, anger, delusion, and profit and support is impossible, and such a one does not fall from the crown. Sariputra, one who reckons a mind of self holds there is a life; because of this cause of clinging to a life, one is drawn by profit and support and hindered in the Way.

Because such people cling wrongly in this way, they cannot even remove the mind greedy for profit and support, much less the subtle afflictions. Sariputra, for one who has penetrated emptiness, to be covered by greed, anger, delusion, and profit and support is utterly impossible, and they do not fall from the crown. Sariputra, one who reckons a self holds that there is truly a life; because of this cause of clinging to a life, one is drawn by profit and support and hindered in the Way.
[Falling from the crown] In the Mahaprajnaparamita Sutra

Chapter on Encouraging Study (Chapter 8): “One who wishes to be fully endowed with such wholesome roots, never to fall into evil realms, never to be reborn in a lowly family, never to dwell in the stage of a sravaka or pratyekabuddha, and never to fall from the crown of a bodhisattva should study Prajnaparamita.”

Sariputra, those who hold the view of self and the view of persons, though they have left home to practice the Way within my Dharma, such foolish people are not truly renunciants within purity. Why? Because they have left home following the Nirgranthas, all reckoning a mind of self and of attainment. Sariputra, one who has attainment has held this view from beginnings time; though one leaves home, it remains unbroken. This is called leaving home through non-Buddhist teachings, not leaving home through the holy Dharma.

Sariputra, those who hold the view of self and the view of persons, though they have left home to practice the Way within my Dharma, such foolish people are not truly renunciants within purity. Why? Because they have left home following the Nirgranthas (non-Buddhist teachers), all reckoning a self and a mind of attainment. Sariputra, one who has attainment has held this view (the view of self, the view of persons) from beginnings time; though one leaves home, this view remains unbroken. This is called leaving home through non-Buddhist teachings, and not leaving home through the holy Dharma.

Why? The base person cannot believe in or delight in the great Dharma, and has no true thought toward the pure great Dharma. Sariputra, because of the causes and conditions of such a heavy crime of destroying the Dharma, the remaining calamity is not exhausted, and they cannot believe in or understand the true characteristics of all dharmas, giving rise to unwholesome karma. Either they slander the eightfold noble path; or toward pure, precept-observing monks they give rise to an evil mind and vainly expose their faults; or they speak of breaking the precepts, breaking right views, breaking right livelihood, breaking dignified deportment; or not seeing another’s faults they vainly stir up right and wrong; or with turbid, angry, and jealous minds they speak ill of others’ good name; or not knowing the meaning and principle of the Buddha’s scriptures they say it is not the Buddha Dharma. Such evil people accomplish the evil karma of destroying the Dharma; within the Buddha’s supreme meaning their minds cannot penetrate, entering and being displeased. Because of the remaining retribution of such heavy crimes, though they diligently practice with vigor, they still cannot take up the characteristic of the object of cognition, much less still the mind to attain the fruit of the Way? Moreover, they deeply rely on the view of self and the view of persons. For those who hold such views, even the Buddhas cannot uproot their root — how much less a sravaka!

Why? These foolish and base people cannot believe in or delight in the great Dharma, and have no true thought toward the pure great Dharma. Sariputra, because of the causes and conditions of such a heavy crime of destroying the Dharma, the remaining calamity is not exhausted, and so they cannot believe in and understand the true characteristics of all dharmas, creating unwholesome karma. Either they slander the eightfold noble path; or toward pure, precept-observing monks they give rise to an evil mind and vainly expose their faults; or they speak of breaking the precepts, breaking right views, breaking right livelihood, breaking dignified deportment; or not seeing another’s faults they vainly stir up right and wrong; or with turbid, angry, and jealous minds they speak ill of others’ good name; or not knowing the meaning and principle of the Buddha’s scriptures they say it is not the Buddha Dharma. Such evil people accomplish the evil karma of destroying the Dharma; within the Buddha’s supreme meaning their minds cannot penetrate, entering and being displeased. Because of the remaining retribution of such heavy crimes, though they diligently practice with vigor, they still cannot take up the characteristic of the object of cognition, much less still the mind to attain the fruit of the Way. Moreover, they deeply rely on the view of self and the view of persons. For those who hold such views, even the Buddhas cannot uproot their root — how much less an arhat!

[The eightfold noble path] That is, the eightfold noble path, also called the eight right paths — the eight paths of the sages: first, right view, that is, correct understanding and seeing. Second, right thought, that is, correct reflection. Third, right speech, that is, correct words. Fourth, right action, that is, correct conduct. Fifth, right livelihood, that is, correct occupation or manner of living. Sixth, right effort, that is, correct diligence. Seventh, right mindfulness, that is, correct contemplation. Eighth, right concentration, that is, correct meditative stillness. By cultivating these eight right paths one may realize the fruit of arhatship. [Breaking right views] Destroying right views (destroying correct understanding and seeing). Master Yinguang said: “The Buddha said that in the world there are two kinds of sinners: one is breaking the precepts, the other is breaking right views. The offense of breaking the precepts is still light, while the offense of breaking right views is very heavy. What is breaking right views? It is just as you said, seeking a future life and not seeking rebirth in the Pure Land; it is a wrong and mistaken view, a wrong view that destroys the Buddha Dharma, and it leads all people to give rise to wrong and mistaken views. Its offense is extremely great and heavy, because the mind is contrary to the Buddha and moreover can mislead all people.” (from the Letter to the Mother of the Layman Zhizheng) [Breaking right livelihood] Destroying right livelihood, that is, not seeking alms or livelihood according to the Dharma and living by wrong livelihood; for example, the five kinds of wrong livelihood: first, appearing with strange signs to seek profit and support; second, speaking of one’s own merits to seek profit and support; third, divining auspicious and inauspicious signs to seek profit and support; fourth, raising one’s voice and displaying authority to seek profit and support; fifth, speaking of the profit one has gained to move people’s minds and so seek profit and support. [Taking up the characteristic of the object of cognition] Earlier, in the second chapter on recollecting the Buddha, the Blessed One said: “Monk, you should take up the characteristic of the object of cognition, bind the mind within the object, and single-mindedly think of the characteristic of emptiness.”

Sariputra, if a person has such unwholesome wrong views of clinging — the view of self, the view of persons, the view of sentient beings, the view of a life, the view of a lifespan — and is again alarmed, doubtful, and afraid toward the supreme-meaning emptiness, know that this person in former lives accomplished the conditions of the crime of destroying the Dharma. Sariputra, if a person clings to evil, wrong, and unwholesome things in this way — clinging to self, clinging to persons, clinging to life — such a person, though a hundred thousand crore Buddhas appear with the threefold teaching, cannot be made to awaken and attain the fruit of the Way. Sariputra, better to cut out one’s tongue with a sharp knife than, not having seen another’s real affairs, to vainly speak of their faults — breaking the precepts, breaking right views, breaking right livelihood, breaking dignified deportment.

Sariputra, if a person has such unwholesome wrong views of clinging — the view of self, the view of persons, the view of sentient beings, the view of a life, the view of a lifespan — and is again alarmed, doubtful, and afraid toward the supreme-meaning emptiness, know that these people in former lives (in their past lives) accomplished the conditions of the crime of destroying the Dharma. Sariputra, these people cling to evil, wrong, and unwholesome things in this way — clinging to self, clinging to persons, clinging to life — and such people, though a hundred thousand crore Buddhas appear with the threefold teaching, cannot be made to awaken and attain the fruit of the Way. Sariputra, better to cut out one’s tongue with a sharp knife than, not having seen another’s real affairs, to vainly speak of their faults — breaking the precepts, breaking right views, breaking right livelihood, breaking dignified deportment.

[The threefold teaching] That is, the three-turn teaching: first, turning the Dharma wheel — after the Buddha attained enlightenment, in the seven years he turned the Dharma wheel of the four noble truths of the Hinayana and spoke of emptiness; second, illuminating the Dharma wheel — after seven years he spoke the Prajnaparamita of the various divisions to make clear emptiness, illuminating existence with emptiness, hence called the illuminating Dharma wheel; third, upholding the Dharma wheel — after thirty years he spoke the Samdhinirmocana Sutra and others, speaking of both emptiness and existence, upholding the two wheels of turning and illuminating, hence called the upholding Dharma wheel.

Sariputra, in future ages there will be monks who well maintain the two hundred fifty precepts. In such persons a mind of pride arises, thinking: ‘I observe the precepts, others do not’; they slight others without any reverence, thinking: ‘I am learned, they are not learned.’ Sariputra, at that time there will be many monks who prize only precepts and practice much the practice of the forest; they can well preserve the precepts, act in accord with what they say, diligently read the scriptures, and seek to penetrate the Buddha Dharma. Such people give rise to the pride of much learning and the pride of the forest dweller, are given to anger, their minds constantly turbid and defiled, deeply harboring a poisonous mind of miserliness, greed, and anger, dull and ignorant, and over a small cause they raise a great matter. Such people, with the mind of anger covering them, mutually expose each other’s faults, saying: breaking the precepts, breaking right views, breaking right livelihood, breaking dignified deportment.

Śāriputra, in the future there will be bhikṣus who well observe the Two Hundred Fifty Precepts. Among these people a mind of self-conceit will arise, and they will think: “I observe the precepts; others do not.” Thus they belittle others, with no reverence in their hearts; they think: “I am learned; others are not learned.” Śāriputra, at that time there will be many bhikṣus who esteem only the observance of the precepts and who much practice the forest-dwelling (araṇya) conduct, who are able to well guard the categories of the precepts and to act in accord with what is taught; who diligently read the scriptures and seek to penetrate the Buddha-dharma. Such people give rise to the conceit of learning and the conceit of forest-dwelling, and yet delight in anger, their minds ever defiled and turbid, deeply harboring the poisonous minds of miserliness, greed, and anger, dull and stubborn and without understanding — and over trivial causes they conjure grave matters. These people, with the poison of anger covering their minds, mutually reproach one another's faults, saying that the other has broken the precepts, broken the views, broken the life, broken the deportment.

[The Two Hundred Fifty Precepts] The complete precepts (upasaṃpanna) of a bhikṣu. [Araṇya conduct] A bhikṣu constantly dwells in the araṇya and does not abide in the world — one of the twelve dhūta (ascetic) practices. [Araṇya] Translated into Chinese as “the place of stillness”; it is a general name for the monasteries where bhikṣus dwell. [Araṇya (ā liàn ruò)] The same as araṇya.

“Śāriputra, in such an assembly there are good bhikṣus whose minds are without partiality and who stand in the middle; yet, dwelling amidst those evil ones, they too join in mutual scorn and dispute without ceasing, unable to sit in meditation or read the scriptures in peace, and both the lay and the home-leavers are disturbed as well. Thus, Śāriputra, at that time there are many bhikṣus — of one year, two years, three years, even up to nine years of ordination — who disrespect the elders and show no reverence. Such people, having left home and received the precepts, act in many ways contrary to the Dharma, and they imitate the upādhyāya and the ācārya likewise without reverence.”

Śāriputra, in such an assembly there are good bhikṣus who, though their minds are without partiality (not taking any side), yet dwelling amidst the evil bhikṣus, they too join with them in mutual scorn and dispute without ceasing, unable to sit in meditation or read the scriptures in peace, and both the lay and the monastic people are disturbed. Thus, Śāriputra, at that time there are many bhikṣus — with one year, two years, three years, even up to nine years of ordination-standing — who disrespect the elders and show no reverence. Though these people have left home and received the precepts, they act in many ways contrary to the Dharma, and toward their upādhyāya and ācārya they likewise show no reverence.

[Ordination-standing (jiè là)] The number of years since a bhikṣu received the complete precepts. [Elder (shàng zuò)] The name of an office in a monastery, ranking just below the abbot. Apart from the abbot, no one stands higher than him, hence the name “elder” (sthavira). Here it refers to those bhikṣus whose ordination-standing is high and who occupy the senior position.

“Śāriputra, at that time the young bhikṣus, and those who had left home earlier but had no one to rely upon, mutually scorned one another. The disciples whom a ten-year bhikṣu has gathered all have no reverence, no deportment, no rules, and likewise act contrary to the Dharma. Śāriputra, at that time those evil people, fully endowed with greed, anger, and delusion, mutually scorned one another, showing no reverence. Because they went against one another, my Dharma is extinguished. Śāriputra, at that time many deluded people committed the karmic offenses of destroying the Dharma, and having committed those offenses, they will fall into the evil destinies.”

Śāriputra, at that time the young bhikṣus, and those who had left home earlier but had no one to rely upon, mutually scorned one another. The disciples whom a ten-year bhikṣu has gathered (per the Vinaya, a bhikṣu must have a full ten years of ordination-standing to gather disciples) — all these disciples have no reverence, no deportment, no rules, and likewise act contrary to the Dharma. Śāriputra, at that time those evil people, fully endowed with greed, anger, and delusion, mutually scorned one another, showing no reverence. Because they went against one another, the true Dharma is extinguished. Śāriputra, at that time many deluded people committed the karmic offenses of destroying the Dharma, and having committed those offenses, they will fall into the evil destinies.

“Śāriputra, I now declare clearly to you: at that time a good bhikṣu who seeks his own benefit should not enter the assembly — not even for a single night — except for an arhat whose defilements are already cut off, and for a sick bhikṣu who has a karmic connection there. Why? Śāriputra, at that time people's poisons of greed, anger, and delusion are strong, and the fear of not being able to stay alive constantly presses upon them. A good person who seeks benefit should always dwell alone in the forests and mountains, in empty stillness, even to the end of life, dying like a wild beast.”

Śāriputra, I now declare clearly to you: at that time a good bhikṣu who seeks his own benefit should not enter the assembly to dwell together with precept-breaking bhikṣus — not even for a single night — unless he himself is an arhat whose defilements are already cut off, or he is a sick bhikṣu who needs care. Why? Śāriputra, at that time people's poisons of greed, anger, and delusion are strong, and the fear of not being able to stay alive constantly presses upon them. All of them pursue fame, gain, and offerings. A good person who seeks his own benefit should always dwell alone in forests and mountains, in empty stillness, even to the end of life, dying like a wild beast, and never dwell together with evil people.
[The fear of not being able to stay alive (bù huó bù wèi)] The fear that one cannot sustain one's own life, causing one to scheme after and hoard wealth.

“Śāriputra, I now declare clearly to you: this true Dharma of mine will not long remain in the world. Why? Because the merit and good roots of sentient beings are exhausted, and the defiled age is near at hand. A good bhikṣu who seeks his own benefit should give rise to such a mind of revulsion: ‘How could I bear to see the Dharma shattered and thrown into disorder, to see this evil world and these troubled times of the renunciates? I should diligently strive with all my heart and soon attain the fruit of the Way.’”

Śāriputra, I now declare clearly to you: my true Dharma cannot long remain in the world. Why? Because the merit and good roots of sentient beings are exhausted, and the defiled and evil age is about to arrive. A good bhikṣu who seeks his own benefit should give rise to such a mind of revulsion: ‘Why should I have to see this true Dharma shattered and thrown into disorder, this evil world and these troubled times of the renunciates? I should diligently strive with all my heart and soon attain the fruit of the Way.’

“Śāriputra, in my Dharma there are no difficult matters. Do not be anxious about clothing, food, bedding, or medicine. You should only diligently practice the Buddha Way and not value the wealth, profit, and offerings of the world. Śāriputra, now listen well; I shall tell you: if there is a bhikṣu who single-mindedly practices the Way, a thousand koṭis of devas will all be of one mind and wish to make offerings to him with all kinds of blissful objects. Śāriputra, the offerings that men make to a bhikṣu who sits in meditation do not compare with those of the devas. Therefore, Śāriputra, you should not worry that you cannot sustain yourselves. When the Buddha's true teaching is given, you should accord with it and practice accordingly. Do not use the emptiness of the supreme meaning to expose the faults of others. Why? Śāriputra, the great danger—
(in ancient usage, the same as “danger”)
namely what is called “the attainment of emptiness.””

Śāriputra, in studying and practicing my Dharma there are no difficult matters. Do not be anxious about clothing, food, bedding, or medicine. You should only diligently practice the Buddha Way and not value the wealth, profit, and offerings of this world. Śāriputra, now listen well; I tell you earnestly: if there is a bhikṣu who single-mindedly practices the Way, a thousand koṭis of devas will all be of one mind and joyfully make offerings to him. Śāriputra, the offerings men make to a bhikṣu who sits in meditation are not equal to those of the devas. Therefore, Śāriputra, do not worry that you cannot sustain yourselves. When the Buddha's true teaching is given, you should accord with it and practice accordingly. Do not use the emptiness of the supreme meaning to expose the faults of others. Why? Śāriputra, the greatest danger is the so-called “attainment of emptiness.”

[Do not use the emptiness of the supreme meaning to expose the faults of others] Do not use the emptiness of the supreme meaning (paramārtha-śūnyatā) to expose the faults of others. If one uses the emptiness of the supreme meaning to expose the faults of others, then one gives rise to the mind of “attainment” within emptiness, and clings to the mark of self and the mark of others. Doing so, one cannot accomplish the supreme Buddha Way; hence it is called “the greatest danger.”

“There may be bhikṣus who, because of my Dharma, have left home and received the precepts, and who diligently strive and progress within this Dharma. Even though the devas and men do not think of them, if they can only single-mindedly and diligently practice the Way, in the end they too will not have to think about the clothing and food they need. Why is that? Because the Tathāgata's store of merit is immeasurable and inexhaustible. Śāriputra, after the Tathāgata's parinirvāṇa, out of the hundred thousand koṭis of portions in the characteristic of the white hair, one portion alone is used to make offerings for the relics and for the disciples. Śāriputra, even if all people in the world were to leave home together and accord with the Dharma in their practice, they could not exhaust even one of the hundred thousand koṭis of portions. Śāriputra, the Tathāgata's merit is thus immeasurable. As for the food and drink and other necessities that the bhikṣus obtain, they will all be amply provided. Śāriputra, these bhikṣus should think in this way and should not, on account of the things they need, engage in wrong kinds of livelihood or evil acts.”

There may be bhikṣus who, because of my Dharma, have left home and received the precepts, and who diligently strive and progress within this Dharma. Even though the devas and men do not come to make offerings, if they can only single-mindedly and diligently practice the Way, in the end they will not lack the clothing and food they need. Why is that? Because the Tathāgata's store of merit is immeasurable and inexhaustible. Śāriputra, after the Tathāgata's parinirvāṇa, out of the hundred thousand koṭis of portions in the characteristic of the white hair, one portion alone is used to make offerings for the relics and for the disciples. Śāriputra, even if all people in the world were to leave home and accord with the true Dharma in their practice, they could never exhaust even one of the hundred thousand koṭis of portions. Śāriputra, the Tathāgata's merit is thus immeasurable. As for the food and drink and other necessities that those bhikṣus obtain, they will all be fully provided. Śāriputra, these bhikṣus should think in this way, and should not, on account of the things they need, engage in wrong kinds of livelihood to sustain their lives.
[Wrong livelihood (xié mìng)] Engaging in improper occupations to sustain one's life.

“Śāriputra, when a bhikṣu wears the patched-robe, he should, upon picking up worn-out clothing from the dust-heap, give rise to this thought: ‘With this I ward off the cold and cultivate the holy Way. Now, with this worn-out garment, I sew and make a saṅghāṭī to wear, and I diligently strive and progress.’ If he is an ordinary person, he should not wear it even for a single night. This bhikṣu, having washed and sewn it clean, wears it. If this bhikṣu gives rise to a mind of greedy clinging toward this patched-robe, then he should immediately abandon it; I do not allow him to wear it, still less other robes. Why? Śāriputra, because in this robe this bhikṣu gives rise to what is not the Dharma of a bhikṣu; this bhikṣu should no longer wear it, still less other things! Śāriputra, at that time it would be better for this bhikṣu to wrap his body in red-hot iron sheets (thin plates of iron) than to wear this patched-robe. Why? Because of his mind of greed and attachment toward this robe. Śāriputra, a bhikṣu of the patched-robe should think: ‘Wearing this patched-robe to ward off the cold and heat and to assist my cultivation of the Way, now I will no longer wear any other robe, and I shall attain the fruit of the stream-enterer, the fruit of the once-returner, the fruit of the non-returner, and the fruit of the arhat.’ Śāriputra, such a patched-robe bhikṣu who exclusively seeks the Way — I allow him to wear it.”

Śāriputra, when a bhikṣu picks up worn-out clothing or scraps of cloth from the dust and refuse, washes them, and makes a patched-robe, then upon wearing it he should give rise to this thought: ‘With this I ward off the cold and cultivate the holy Way; I should diligently strive and progress.’ If his mind is that of an ordinary person, then he should not wear it even for a single night. If this bhikṣu gives rise to a mind of greedy clinging toward this patched-robe, then he should take it off (because greed and clinging are the mind of an ordinary person); I do not allow him to wear it, still less other robes. Why? Śāriputra, because in this robe this bhikṣu gives rise to what is not the Dharma of a bhikṣu (he gives rise to a mind contrary to the Dharma); this bhikṣu should no longer wear this patched-robe, still less other garments! Śāriputra, at that time it would be better for this bhikṣu to wrap his body in red-hot thin plates of iron than to wear this patched-robe. Why? Because of his mind of greed and attachment toward this robe. Śāriputra, a bhikṣu who wears the patched-robe should think: ‘Wearing this patched-robe to ward off cold and heat and to assist my cultivation of the Way, now I will no longer wear any other robe, and I shall attain the fruit of the stream-enterer, the fruit of the once-returner, the fruit of the non-returner, and the fruit of the arhat.’ Śāriputra, such a patched-robe bhikṣu who single-mindedly seeks the Way — I allow him to wear it.

[Patched-robe (nà yī)] Also called the dust-heap robe (pāṃśukūla); it is the Dharma-robe made by picking up worn-out clothing or scraps of cloth discarded in the dust and refuse, washing them, and cutting and sewing them. [Saṅghāṭī] Here it refers to the patched-robe. [Ordinary person (pṛthagjana)] An ordinary person who is deluded about the principles of things and who transmigrates through birth and death. [Iron plate (tiě yè) (
yè
)] A thin sheet of iron.

“Śāriputra, a bhikṣu who begs for alms should be without discrimination among all dharmas. He should constantly gather his mind and not let it become scattered when entering a village, adorning himself with all the dhyānas. Having obtained his alms, his mind undefiled, he carries the food he has received out of the village. At a place beside pure water where the Way can be cultivated, he sets the food to one side, washes his feet, and sits. Placing the food before him, he should give rise to the perception of revulsion, the perception of impurity, the perception of urine and feces, the perception of stench and decay, the perception of vomiting, the perception of smeared sores, the perception of loathing, the perception of the flesh of one's own child, the perception of a foul fruit, the perception of heaviness; and within his body he should give rise to the perception of death, the perception of bluishness, the perception of pus, the perception of decay and ruin.”

Śāriputra, a bhikṣu who begs for alms should be without discrimination among all dharmas. He should constantly gather his mind and not let it become scattered when entering a village, adorning himself with all the dhyānas. Having finished begging for alms, his mind undefiled, he carries the food he has obtained out of the village. At a place beside pure water where the Way can be cultivated, he sets the food to one side, washes his feet, and sits. Before eating, he should give rise to the perception of revulsion, the perception of impurity, the perception of urine and feces, the perception of stench and decay, the perception of vomiting, the perception of smeared sores, the perception of loathing, the perception of the flesh of one's own child, the perception of a foul fruit, the perception of heaviness; and within his body he should give rise to the perception of death, the perception of bluishness, the perception of pus, the perception of decay and ruin.
[Village (jù luò)] A hamlet or village — the place where a throng of people gathers and dwells.

“Śāriputra, a bhikṣu should give rise to such a thought, and only then eat with a mind free of greed and clinging — merely to sustain his body and remove the afflictions of hunger and thirst, so that he can cultivate the Way. He should think: ‘In eating this food, I break my former suffering and do not give rise to future suffering; my mind attains joy, is well-tempered and free of harm, my body becomes light and agile, and my steps are peaceful.’ And he should think: ‘Having eaten this food, I should attain the fruit of the stream-enterer, the fruit of the once-returner, the fruit of the non-returner, the fruit of the arhat, and the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas.’ Śāriputra, a bhikṣu who eats thus — I allow him to beg for alms. Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu who begs for alms, toward the food he has obtained, gives rise to a mind greedy for flavor, regarding it as sweet and delicious, and thinks: ‘In eating this food I shall gain a good complexion and abundant strength’ — but does not think: ‘In eating this food I diligently practice the holy Way’ — such a bhikṣu I do not allow even to receive a single sip of water, still less a meal.”

Śāriputra, this bhikṣu should give rise to such a thought, and only then eat with a mind free of greed and clinging — merely to sustain his body and remove the afflictions of hunger and thirst, so that he can cultivate the Way. He should think: ‘In eating this food, I break my former suffering and do not give rise to future suffering; my mind attains joy, is well-tempered and free of harm, my body becomes light and agile, and my steps are peaceful.’ And he should think: ‘Having eaten this food, I should attain the fruit of the stream-enterer, the fruit of the once-returner, the fruit of the non-returner, the fruit of the arhat, and the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas.’ Śāriputra, a bhikṣu who eats thus — I allow him to beg for alms. Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu who begs for alms, toward the food he has obtained, gives rise to a mind greedy for flavor, regarding it as sweet and delicious, and thinks: ‘In eating this food I shall gain a good complexion and abundant strength’ — but does not think: ‘In eating this food I diligently practice the holy Way’ — such a bhikṣu I do not allow even to receive a single cup of water, still less a meal.
[Patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (wú shēng fǎ rěn)] This is the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

“Śāriputra, if one does not see the faults in food, does not see the way out of it, and yet still eats, then it would be better to cut one's own thigh-flesh with one's hand and eat it. Why? I allow the practitioner and the one who has attained to receive the offerings of others; I do not allow others. Śāriputra, what is meant by ‘practitioner’? If a bhikṣu is resolved to cut off the fetters in this life and to enter the nirvāṇa without remainder, cultivating the holy Way as if extinguishing the blaze on his own head, and also cuts off the unwholesome evil dharmas — this is called a ‘practitioner.’ And whoever single-mindedly understands and believes in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, so as to attain the fruit of the stream-enterer, the fruit of the once-returner, the fruit of the non-returner, and the fruit of the arhat, cutting off all the defilements — this is called a ‘practitioner.’ Whoever seeks all good dharmas, always going to inquire about them — this is called a ‘practitioner.’ And whoever can give rise to the resolve to liberate all beings — this is called a ‘practitioner.’ Whoever diligently cultivates all the aids to the Way and, in the various scriptures, practices as is taught, and whoever single-mindedly seeks the Buddha Way — Śāriputra, in the Buddha-dharma these are called ‘practitioners.’ What is meant by ‘the one who has attained’? One who has attained the fruit of the stream-enterer and is freed from the three evil destinies is called ‘the one who has attained.’ The once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat, having cut off all the defilements, their seeking of the Way has come to rest, what was to be done has been done, and they have well studied the three trainings — these are called ‘those who have attained.’ I allow such people to receive offerings. If such a person receives offerings, that is called ‘well receiving offerings.’

Śāriputra, if one does not see one's own faults in food, does not see the way out of birth and death, and yet still eats, then it would be better to cut one's own thigh-flesh with one's hand and eat it. Why? I allow the practitioner and the one who has attained to receive the offerings of others; I do not allow others. Śāriputra, what is meant by ‘practitioner’? If a bhikṣu is resolved to cut off the fetters and outflows in this life and to enter the nirvāṇa without remainder, cultivating the holy Way as if dousing the blaze on his own head, and also cuts off the unwholesome evil dharmas — this is called a ‘practitioner.’ And whoever single-mindedly understands and believes in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, so as to attain the fruit of the stream-enterer, the fruit of the once-returner, the fruit of the non-returner, and the fruit of the arhat, cutting off all the defilements — this is called a ‘practitioner.’ Whoever seeks all good dharmas, always going to inquire about them — this is called a ‘practitioner.’ And whoever can give rise to the resolve to liberate all beings — this is called a ‘practitioner.’ Whoever diligently cultivates all the aids to the Way and, in the various scriptures, practices as is taught, and whoever single-mindedly seeks the Buddha Way — Śāriputra, in the Buddha-dharma these are called ‘practitioners.’ What is meant by ‘the one who has attained’? One who has attained the fruit of the stream-enterer and is freed from the three evil destinies is called ‘the one who has attained.’ The once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat, having cut off all the defilements, their seeking of the Way has come to rest, what was to be done has been done, and they have well studied the three trainings — these are called ‘those who have attained.’ I allow such people to receive offerings. If such a person receives offerings, that is called ‘well receiving offerings.’

[Fetters and outflows (jié shǐ)] The fetters (saṃyojana) and the outflows (anuśaya). Both ‘fetters’ and ‘outflows’ are alternative names for the defilements. The defilements can bind body and mind and form the fruits of suffering, hence they are called ‘fetters’; and they can cause sentient beings to sink in the bitter sea of birth and death, hence they are also called ‘outflows.’ There are nine fetters and ten outflows. [The nine fetters] The fetter of love (greed and craving), the fetter of anger (ill-will), the fetter of pride (arrogance), the fetter of delusion (stupidity), the fetter of doubt (doubt about the true Dharma), the fetter of views (the view of self, extreme views, wrong views, and so forth), the fetter of grasping (grasping at views and grasping at precepts, falsely reckoning and clinging), the fetter of miserliness (hoarding wealth), and the fetter of envy (envying others). The ten outflows are also called the ten delusions, or the ten root defilements, namely: 1. greed — craving for the five desires; 2. anger — ill-will without forbearance; 3. delusion — stupidity and ignorance; 4. pride — arrogance and self-importance; 5. doubt — skepticism and unbelief; 6. the view of self — grasping at the body of the five aggregates; 7. extreme views — grasping at the two views of eternalism and annihilism; 8. wrong views — slandering cause and effect as nonexistent and destroying all good deeds; 9. the view of views-grasping — holding fixed opinions, reckoning that which is not fruit as fruit; 10. the view of precepts-and-observances-grasping — holding improper precepts, reckoning that which is not cause as cause. The first five are the five dull outflows; the latter five are the five sharp outflows. ‘Outflow’ is an alternative name for the defilement, because the defilements cause sentient beings to drift through birth and death.

[Nirvāṇa without remainder (wú yú niè pán)] The two delusions — the delusion of views and the delusion of thought — together with the body of the five aggregates one has received, are all completely extinguished with nothing left over; this is called the nirvāṇa without remainder. [Aids to the Way (zhù dào)] The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right exertions, and the rest — the thirty-seven kinds of aids (bodhipākṣika dharmas) — can support calm-abiding and insight, hence they are called ‘aids to the Way.’ They can also support the virtues of the fruit, and the various practices support one another, hence they are called ‘aids to the Way.’ [The thirty-seven aids to the Way (sān shí qī dào pǐn)] Also called the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa dharmas): the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right exertions, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. Their number is altogether thirty-seven items, and they are the important provisions for cultivating the Way; hence the name ‘the thirty-seven aids to the Way.’ [The three trainings (sān xué)] The training in morality, the training in concentration, and the training in wisdom. Morality (śīla) is the precepts — what the Vinaya-piṭaka expounds — and can prevent people from creating all the evil karma of body, speech, and mind. Concentration (samādhi) is meditation — what the Sūtra-piṭaka expounds — and can enable people to quiet their reflections and clarify their minds. Wisdom (prajñā) is insight — what the Abhidharma-piṭaka expounds — and can enable people to discover the truth and cut off delusion. Cultivating these three trainings, one may, from morality, attain concentration; from concentration, develop wisdom; and in the end attain the undefiled fruit of the Way. Therefore the three trainings are also called ‘the three undefiled trainings.’ [Undefiled (wú lòu)] ‘Outflow’ (lòu) is an alternative name for the defilements, bearing the meaning of leaking or seeping out. ‘Undefiled’ (anāsrava) means pure and free of defilements.

“Śāriputra, those of pure precept-keeping, those who convert the donors, and those who are learned and recite the scriptures — that is, those who recite the sūtra, the geya, the records (vyākaraṇa), the gāthā, the udāna, the nidāna, and so on through all the scriptures, the jātaka, the vaipulya, the adbhuta-dharma, the avadāna, and the upadeśa — such people, being able also to keep the precepts purely without flaw or blemish, neither defiled nor turbid, free and unattached, praised by the wise, complete within themselves, and accordant with dhyāna, delighting at all times in sitting in meditation — such bhikṣus I also allow to receive offerings.”

Śāriputra, those of pure precept-keeping, those who transform and convert the donors, and those who are learned and recite the twelve divisions of the scriptures — such people, being able also to keep the precepts purely without flaw or blemish, neither defiled nor turbid, free and unattached, praised by the wise, complete within themselves, and accordant with dhyāna, delighting at all times in sitting in meditation — such bhikṣus I also allow to receive offerings.

[Sūtra, geya, records, gāthā, udāna, nidāna, jātaka, vaipulya, adbhuta-dharma, avadāna, upadeśa] These are the respective names of the twelve divisions of scriptures. [The twelve divisions of scriptures] All the dharmas spoken by the Buddha, according to the differences in the literary form of the scriptures and in the matters and characteristics they record, may be divided from the three piṭakas into twelve names; collectively they are called ‘the twelve divisions of the three piṭakas.’ In general they are called ‘all the scriptures’; in particular they are called ‘the twelve divisions.’ These twelve are: 1. Sūtra, translated into Chinese as ‘the scripture that accords’ — the long-line prose texts within the scriptures that directly set forth the meaning of the Dharma; hence also called ‘the long-line scripture.’ 2. Geya, translated into Chinese as ‘re-recital’ or ‘responsive recital’ — verses that recite again in verse form the meaning of the long-line prose text of the preceding scripture; such verses are called ‘the re-recital scripture.’ 3. Vyākaraṇa, translated into Chinese as ‘the record (prophecy)’ — whenever in a scripture the Buddha gives a bodhisattva the prophecy that he shall certainly become a Buddha in the future, gives a pratyekabuddha the prophecy that he shall attain the Way in a later life, gives a śrāvaka the prophecy that he shall attain the Way in a future life, and records the retributions that other beings of the six destinies shall undergo in a later life — this is called ‘the record scripture.’ 4. Gāthā, translated into Chinese as ‘recitation’ or ‘a verse standing alone’ — a scripture that does not depend on long-line prose but directly displays the dharmas in verses, such as the Dharmapada (Faju Jing) and so forth; it is called ‘the recitation scripture.’ 5. Udāna, translated into Chinese as ‘spoken of itself’ or ‘the scripture spoken without being asked’ — whenever, with no one asking, the Buddha of himself proclaims such scriptural passages as the Amitābha Sūtra (Amituo Jing); it is called ‘the spoken-of-itself scripture.’ 6. Nidāna, translated into Chinese as ‘the scripture of conditions’ or ‘the scripture of dependent origination’ — since the Tathāgata's preaching of the Dharma always has conditions, that is, the conditions of seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma recorded in the scriptures, and the circumstances from beginning to end of the Buddha's preaching and transforming teaching, as in the ‘Prologue’ sections of the various scriptures; hence it is called ‘the scripture of conditions.’ 7. Avadāna, translated into Chinese as ‘parable’ — whenever parables are told in the scriptures and the Vinaya, and by the parable the meaning of the Dharma is displayed; hence it is called ‘the parable scripture.’ 8. Itivṛttaka, translated into Chinese as ‘the deeds of former times’ or ‘the thus-spoken scripture’ — the texts within the scriptures that tell of the karmic deeds and histories of disciples, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas in their past lives, and the circumstances of the instruction urging them to diligent practice in seeking the Way and liberation; hence it is called ‘the deeds of former times scripture.’ 9. Jātaka, the birth-story scripture — whenever within a scripture the Buddha tells of the circumstances of his own conduct when, in the past, he practiced the bodhisattva Way, cultivated all the ascetic practices, and benefited sentient beings; it is called ‘the birth-story scripture.’ 10. Vaipulya, translated into Chinese as ‘the expansive’ — the general name for all the Mahāyāna scriptures; it also refers to scriptures whose words are broad and whose principles are correct, and which broadly discriminate the profound truth of all dharmas. Such scriptures are called ‘the expansive scripture.’ 11. Adbhuta-dharma, translated into Chinese as ‘the never-before-had’ — the scriptures that tell of the body-measures of the devas, the quaking of the great earth, things rare since ancient times, and the inconceivable power of the Buddha; it is called ‘the never-before-had scripture.’ 12. Upadeśa, translated into Chinese as ‘discussion’ — when the various scriptures spoken by the Buddha, treated as discussions, questions and answers, and the discrimination of principle, are discriminated and spoken at length, then they are called ‘the discussion scripture.’

“Śāriputra, one who has personally realized the Dharma has no doubt or regret. I allow such a person to ascend the high seat and expound the Dharma. Though still an ordinary person, if he purely observes the precepts, if his mind does not greedily cling to the scriptural meanings of non-Buddhist paths, if he single-mindedly and diligently seeks the supreme fruit of the renunciates, if he does not covet profit and offerings, and with skillful flexibility and fixed exposition is learned, broadly illustrating as vast as the great ocean, and even if he should lose his life would not speak falsely, takes no pleasure in disputes and litigation, benefiting himself and others, and speaks only the pure and supreme true meaning, then what he says being thus, so also does he practice — Śāriputra, such a speaker I allow to expound the Dharma.”

Śāriputra, one who has personally realized the Dharma has no doubt or regret regarding the true reality of all dharmas. I allow such people to ascend the high seat and expound the Dharma. Though still ordinary persons, if they purely observe the precepts, if their minds do not greedily cling to the scriptural meanings of non-Buddhist paths, if they single-mindedly and diligently seek the supreme fruit of the renunciates, if they do not covet profit and offerings, and with skillful flexibility and fixed exposition are learned, broadly illustrating as vast as the great ocean, and even if they should lose their lives would not speak falsely, take no pleasure in disputes and litigation, benefiting themselves and others, and speak only the pure and supreme true meaning, then what they say being thus, so also do they practice — Śāriputra, such speakers I allow to expound the Dharma.

[One who has personally realized the Dharma (shēn zhèng fǎ zhě)] ‘Personally’ (shēn) here means ‘in one's own body — firsthand.’ The Buddha-dharma is extremely profound; only through realization can it be known. Therefore the Buddha said: ‘One who has personally realized the Dharma has no doubt or regret; I allow such a person to ascend the high seat and expound the Dharma.’ [Ordinary person (pṛthagjana)] Here ‘ordinary person’ is spoken in contrast to the noble ones. Those at or above the first fruit of the Lesser Vehicle (the stream-enterer), and those at or above the first-ground bodhisattva of the Great Vehicle, are the noble ones; those below them, who have not yet cut off their delusion, are ordinary persons.

“What the Tathāgata speaks can make the various dharmas not contradict one another — that is, he speaks of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge-and-vision of liberation. Śāriputra, a bhikṣu who seeks profit, who has left home for the Buddha's sake yet breaks the categories of the precepts — of what use is his preaching the Dharma! Why? Śāriputra, in my scriptures it is said: if a person is not himself good and still, and cannot himself guard himself, yet is able to make others good and still and self-guarded — there is no such case. As when a person himself sinks in the mud, yet wishes to pull others out — there is no such case. If a person can himself be good and still, can himself come out of the mud, and wishes to pull others out — then there is such a case.”

What the Tathāgata speaks can make the various dharmas not contradict one another — that is, he speaks of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge-and-vision of liberation. Śāriputra, a bhikṣu who pursues fame, gain, and offerings, who has left home as a disciple of the Buddha yet breaks the categories of the precepts — how can he preach the Dharma! Why? Śāriputra, in my scriptures it is said: if a person is not himself good and still, and cannot guard himself against the defilements and attractions of the objects of sense, yet would go to teach and transform others to be good and still and self-guarded — that is impossible (there is no such case). This is like one who is himself about to be drowned in the swamp, yet would still pull others out of the swamp — impossible. If a person can himself be good and still, can himself come out of the swamp, and would go to rescue others — then it is possible (there is such a case).

[Good and still (shàn jì)] To be free from desire and still. The Sutra of the Forty-Two Chapters spoken by the Buddha says: ‘When the World-Honored One had accomplished the Way, he thought thus: to be free of desire and to be still is the most excellent.’

“Therefore, Śāriputra, I now declare clearly to you: to slander the Tathāgata is no light offense. A bhikṣu of truthful speech should be allowed to expound the Dharma, for a precept-keeping bhikṣu who does not speak falsely is able to make the Dharma-gift. Śāriputra, to ascend the high seat and expound the Dharma, with certainty cutting off doubts, is the most supreme of affairs; if one's precept-keeping is impure and one clings to the meanings of non-Buddhist paths, I do not allow it. And the liar, the one who prizes worldly pleasures, the one who seeks profit and offerings, the one who delights in disputes — these too I do not allow. I allow those of pure precept-keeping, those of upright and straightforward minds, those who have penetrated the true reality of all dharmas, to ascend the high seat and expound the Dharma. Śāriputra, a precept-breaking bhikṣu would do better to give up his precepts entirely than to wear the appearance of a sage, to use the kāṣāya to conceal the defilement of his offenses, and in secret to commit all kinds of evil while receiving the faithful offerings of others. Śāriputra, by these trivial causes he will for a long, long time receive an existence in hell.”

Therefore, Śāriputra, I now declare clearly to you: to slander the Tathāgata is no light offense. A bhikṣu of truthful speech should be allowed to expound the Dharma, for a precept-keeping bhikṣu who does not speak falsely is able to make the Dharma-gift. Śāriputra, to ascend the high seat and expound the Dharma, with its meanings determined and cutting off the doubts of sentient beings, is the most supreme of affairs; if one's precept-keeping is impure and one clings to the scriptural meanings of non-Buddhist paths, I do not allow them to expound the Dharma. And the liar, the one who prizes worldly pleasures, the one who seeks profit and offerings, the one who delights in disputes — these too I do not allow. I allow those of pure precept-keeping, those of upright and straightforward minds, those who have penetrated the true reality of all dharmas, to ascend the high seat and expound the Dharma. Śāriputra, a precept-breaking bhikṣu would do better to give up his precepts than to falsely assume the appearance of the holy order, to use the kāṣāya to conceal the defilement of his offenses, and in secret to commit all kinds of evil while receiving the faithful offerings of others. Śāriputra, by doing so, by these trivial causes, he will for a long, long time receive an existence in hell.
[Faithful offering (xìn shī)] The gift (alms) given by a person of faith.

blocks.text: Appendix: Instructions to the Assembly at the Commencement of the Seven-Day Period of Vigorous Recitation

inline.s: Master Xingce, the Tenth Patriarch of the Pure Land School

In reciting the Name for seven days, the key lies in single-minded, unconfused recitation, unbroken and unmixed; it is not necessarily that swift recitation and much recitation are superior. Only do not be slow and do not be hasty; recite the Name closely and continuously, so that the Buddha-name in the mind is clear and distinct, each one discernible. Whether dressing or eating, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, this one great Name is continuous and unbroken, like breath itself — neither scattered nor sinking. To recite the Name thus may be called one who is able to be single-minded and vigorous in practice.
If you are truly a follower of the Way
(a follower of the Way, i.e., one who studies the Way)
, and can directly observe and investigate that all dharmas are “thus”
(“thus” — together with dharma-nature and reality — are all alternative names for the true reality of all dharmas)
, with no two marks. What are called “sentient being”
(sentient beings)
and Buddha are non-dual; self and other are non-dual; the reliant and the reliant-being are non-dual; purity and defilement are non-dual; suffering and joy are non-dual; rejoicing
(a variant of “to rejoice”)
and loathing are non-dual; taking and rejecting are non-dual; bodhi and affliction are non-dual; birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are non-dual. All these pairs

(that is, the pairs of sentient being and Buddha, self and other, the reliant and the reliant-being, purity and defilement, suffering and joy, rejoicing and loathing, taking and rejecting, bodhi and affliction, birth-and-death and nirvāṇa)
are all of a single mark, one Way pure and clean. There is no need to force the disposing and arranging
(disposing, arranging)

; only then, with trueness itself, observe and investigate. When this investigation reaches its utmost, suddenly it accords with one's original mind. Then you know that dressing and eating are always samādhi; that laughter and joking, anger and scolding, are none other than Buddha-work; that a single mind and a scattered mind are ultimately idle talk. Throughout the entire day and night, you cannot find so much as a hair's breadth of an “other” mark. Although you recite with utmost mind
(a variant of “to recite”)

, it is the same as mouthing abuse at will; and although you diligently cultivate and uphold, it too is ascetic practice within a dream. Only by thus fully understanding do you become a genuine student of the Way who single-mindedly and vigorously recites the Name.

[The reliant and the reliant-being (yī zhèng)] The dependent retribution and the primary retribution. The lands, houses, utensils, and so forth of the world, on which the body relies, are called the ‘dependent retribution’; the body of sentient beings, a temporary combination of the five aggregates and the result of karma created in the past, is called the ‘primary retribution.’
The first single-mindedness
(reciting the Name with a single-minded, unconfused mind)
seems difficult but is easy; the latter single-mindedness
(the accord with one's original mind)

seems easy but is difficult. But the one who can attain the first single-mindedness is certain of rebirth in the Pure Land; the one who can also attain the latter single-mindedness can reach the highest grade. Yet these two kinds of single-mindedness are both matters for the common person of the vast earth; whoever has a mind can cultivate and study them. The monks and laity gathered together here in the same hall
(the monastics and the lay)

must not exalt the holy states too high and contentedly place themselves in the inferior. Each must diligently spur on his body and mind — within the shortest span, the seven days; at the farthest, one whole life — always harboring such faith, always cultivating such practice. Even if you do not realize and attain
(even if you fail to realize this state)
, the cause is still strong, and the grade of the lotus-bud palace
(the grade of one's rebirth by transformation within the lotus bud)
will certainly not fall in the middle or low. If, however, after the seven days, you turn a deaf ear and leave it unheeded, and the familiar place
(referring to emotional attachment)
after all does not come to birth, and the place of birth
(referring to the recitation of the Buddha-name)

remains hard to ripen, then ignorance and the karmic habits, pulling and entangling, only wish to claim merit for these seven days — and these seven days have not even reached the ground of single-minded, unconfused recitation. This is precisely what is called ‘few roots of good, little merit, and thin conditions’ — how can one hope for rebirth in that land? To the point that the golden-mouthed, sincere words turn rather into suspicion of deceit — whose fault is that? All gathered in these seven days of pure practice, may each examine himself, and admonish and encourage one another.

[The affairs of the common person of the vast earth (bó dì fán fū)] The affairs on the side of the ‘common person of the vast earth.’ The common person of the vast earth, also called the common person of the thin earth, refers to the stage of the ordinary person. [Thin earth (bó dì)] ‘Thin’ (bó) means ‘pressed upon’; the ‘thin earth’ is the state pressed upon by all the many sufferings, that is, the realm of the ordinary person. The Contemplation of the Pure Mind (Jingxin Jieguan) says: ‘The common person of the thin earth has a foul body, mean and lowly, and his retribution is base and inferior.’
(The above is recorded from Master Xingce’s Pure Land Exhortative Sayings.)
